speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter which is both pressing and urgent. Given that Canada's inflation rate has increased by S'A per cent in one year, and given that the government's high interest rate policy, which was supposed to slow down inflation, is obviously not working, but is instead causing untold hardship to small businesses, farmers, and those on fixed incomes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm):
That the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance devise a fair and practical policy to halt the growth of inflation, and abandon their love affair with the Governor of the Bank of Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been brought to my attention that VIA Rail is considering cancelling as many as 16 commuter routes in Canada. One of these routes is the passenger service between Havelock, Peterborough and Toronto. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Van-koughnet):
That none of these routes be terminated in light of the recent Ontario task force report on provincial rail policy, and that serious consideration be given by VIA Rail to extending commuter service, not reducing it, at a time when energy conservation should be the number one priority.

speechtext:

Credit should therefore be given for every possible start in order to alleviate this embarrassment. Since the senior citizens' home at 551 Hugel Avenue in Midland, Ontario, is being constructed under a building permit issued November 6, 1980, with CMHC funds, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm):
That the federal government's construction sign outside the building be updated to delete the designation of the hon. member for Papineau as the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a post he has not occupied since March 20, 1979, and insert the name of the hon. member for York-Scarborough who has been responsible for CMHC since March 3, 1980.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that in Burnaby, British Columbia, Nabob Foods Limited has substantially reduced its work force, eliminating over 150 jobs and cutting product lines since FIRA approved their takeover by a Swiss multinational Jacobs AG in 1976, and in view of the fact that in recent months union members at the Burnaby plant had to endure a union busting unfair labour practice in an attempt to prevent Jacobs from clawing back gains made under earlier contracts, and in view of the fact that the Foreign Investment Review Agency is a toothless wonder not mandated to protect the job security of Canadian workers

June 30, 1981
employed at plants affected by foreign takeovers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce take immediate action to insist that foreign companies make long-term commitments to jobs in Canada by amending the Foreign Investment Review Agency Act, and take steps to put an end to the massive loss of jobs at the Burnaby Nabob plant.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board, the minister responsible for disruptions of services in the Public Service of Canada. After a long period in which Radio-Canada and CBC have been on strike we now have a situation in which some 23,000 postal clerks and mail handlers are out on strike today. When we take account of the fact that last fall some 48,000 clerks were out, that means that in the last eight months alone nearly one quarter of the public servants under the direct authority of the President of the Treasury Board have been out on strike. That indicates a terrible record of labour relations by this government.

June 30, 1981
Oral Questions
Now that that record has deprived Canadians of the right to receive their mail, may I ask the President of the Treasury Board what action he plans to take now to bring an end to this postal strike before it can cause real and deep damage to Canadians in all walks of life?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am frankly hurt by the comments of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition with respect to my record in negotiating settlements. I might refer him to an article in the Toronto Star-
Oh, oh!

This is a quotation from William Doherty, who is the first vice-president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. He says:
-"dozens and dozens" of disagreements between the government and its workers are settled peacefully under the collective bargaining system.
The public's attention isn't drawn to these because "the only time the media pays any attention is when things get down to the wire and there's a major strike threatened."
For example, there was practically no media interest recently when ... an agreement between the government and 19,000 of its blue collar workers across the country-
Was reached.
Hear, hear!
I think the government is in fact to be congratulated for the record it has in the settling of disputes in the public sector.

Madam Speaker, this government is unbelievable. The minister stands up in this House and says he is hurt. The people who are hurt by his actions are elderly Canadians, small businesses and others who count upon their mail service, a service which has been denied them by the incompetence of this government.
Any minister who could stand and be proud of having one quarter of the people who work under his authority out on strike in eight months is a minister who deserves to resign immediately.
The minister knows that the difference between the government's offer last Friday and the cost of the conciliation board report is less than 2 per cent, and yet the government maintained that the board's recommendation could not even form the basis of negotiations. The minister also knows that his best chance of a settlement at less than that extra 2 per cent was to negotiate to a settlement before a strike, and that the longer the strike goes on the higher the cost will be to Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, will the President of the Treasury Board explain to this House of Commons why he deliberately provoked a strike which is going to wreak such havoc on so many Canadians when he knows that a settlement was available and that a
settlement later will cost the government and the people much more than a settlement would have this past weekend?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is not inhibited by facts. I will give him a few facts, in the event Your Honour offers him an opportunity of asking another supplementary question.
In fact the position of the union has been that it will not return to the bargaining table unless every element of the recommendations of the chairman of the conciliation board is accepted. That would produce an increase in the over-all rate, as indicated by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition-an increase, incidentally, which would take us into a very high range of settlements across the country, which would be a very serious matter indeed. However, going beyond that, I have with me a letter from the president of the union, who says that having accepted that and then returning to the table, we will begin to negotiate the questions raised in the union minority report of Mr. Desmarais.
That report embraces such things as wages, for example, where Mr. Desmarais recommended that there be an untriggered COLA, which automatically gives us a rate of something in the neighbourhood of 13 per cent because it is compounded on a quarterly basis as the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition knows, plus the settlement itself which was requested, that would bring the over-all rate to 22.58 per cent. I am surprised that the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, concerned as he pretends to be about restraint and the deficit, would even suggest that we should negotiate a settlement on that basis.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, it is no wonder that we have no postal service in the country starting today, when we have the minister responsible for negotiating the government side who has twice in the House misrepresented publicly the position of the union. Perhaps it is because he knows it is not the most popular union in the country and he is looking for a scapegoat upon whom he can blame the inefficiency of his government.
i
Oh, oh!
The minister has not yet explained what he intends to do to ensure that Canadians have the benefit of their postal service.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Postmaster General. He will remember that when post office strikes were averted, either last year by this Postmaster General or the year before by the hon. member for Vancouver South, they were avoided by the direct involvement of the Postmaster General. Will the Postmaster General tell the House why he has not taken a direct role in trying to avoid this strike, as he did last year?
June 30, 1981



Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs and Postmaster General): Madam Speaker, I want to say to the Leader of the Official Opposition that so far the Treasury Board has conducted the negotiations in impeccable fashion, and I find it altogether deplorable that the Canadian Union of Postal Workers has refused to pursue the negotiations and is now in a position to strike. Keeping in mind the generous offers made by the Treasury Board on behalf of the government, I suggest that the attitude of the leaders of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers is inexplicable. Rather than launching into this war of words which reflects a blatant lack of responsibility on the part of the Leader of the Opposition, members opposite would be much better advised to urge the postal workers to return to the negotiation table with a view to ending the current postal strike through a negotiated settlement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXCLUSION OF POSTMASTER GENERAL FROM NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, for the third time today a minister has refused to answer a question. The minister knows that when governments wanted a postal settlement in the past and not a strike, they sent in the Postmaster General to negotiate. That was not done this time. Why, when it was done successfully on the last two occasions, was it not done this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: EXCLUSION OF POSTMASTER GENERAL FROM NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, periodically we have reached settlements with several unions of the Post Office Department without strike action on their part. Quite recently the Treasury Board reached a settlement with postal carriers through the normal negotiation process without the need for a strike. I have no reason to claim at this time that there are not enough elements on the negotiation table to enable us to arrive at a negotiated settlement, to the extent where the leaders of the Canadian union of Postal Workers are prepared to discuss conscientiously and responsibly with the negotiating unit of the Canadian government. Madam Speaker, I would suggest to the Leader of the Official Opposition that, instead of trying to score political points and acting as a petty demagogue, he ought to recommend to the postal leaders that they resume negotiations.

subtopic: CONTENTS OF GOVERNMENT'S OFFER TO UNION
CONTENTS OF GOVERNMENT'S OFFER TO UNION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board who has made some allegations about the existing position of the negotiations. Yesterday in the House the minister indicated that the government was presenting a final offer yesterday, "a
Oral Questions
full package on all outstanding issues." The minister maintains that the reason we do not have negotiations is because the union will not negotiate. Why did the government's offer yesterday contain for the first time matters which had not been recommended by its nominee or by itself? In other words, why was the offer made yesterday worse than any previous offer made to the union?
I refer specifically to the fact that the offer contained roll-back provisions, taking away rights granted in previous contracts, roll-back provisions which had not been previously demanded by the government or by its nominee in this round of bargaining. Since the minister says he believes in bargaining in good faith, why was bargaining in such bad faith entered into yesterday? Why should the people of Canada believe that the offer was made with any other intent than to create a strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: CONTENTS OF GOVERNMENT'S OFFER TO UNION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am sure the people of Canada will accept our view and our word; we had no intention of creating a strike.

subtopic: CONTENTS OF GOVERNMENT'S OFFER TO UNION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTENTS OF GOVERNMENT'S OFFER TO UNION
speechtext:
Moreover, I point out to the hon. member the reason the package was delivered was that we had no other way of communicating with the union. The union left the negotiating room on Friday and we invited them back to the negotiating table. I have already answered why they did not come back-because they said there was a pre-condition. The only way we could convey the position we had on these various elements was to put them into a package and send it to them, hoping that those elements would form the basis of negotiation. The normal course would be to sit down then at the table with their position, as I have explained it to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, and negotiate a satisfactory settlement. The union has categorically refused to do that to date.
I share the wish of my colleague, the Postmaster General, that the union will reconsider its position, particularly in view of the major movement which we made in terms of paid marternity leave, and return to the table and negotiate a satisfactory settlement immediately.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister knows full well that the offer which was made yesterday is worse than the offer which was made last week. That is never the basis for entering into good faith bargaining at this late stage, as he will find out if he checks with the Minister of Labour.

Madam Speaker, given that the minister has refused to enter into negotiations in good faith, and given that the spread between the two parties in real dollar terms is about 2 per cent-and those are Treasury Board figures-can the minister tell us whether the Treasury Board has costed the effect of this strike to Canadians in all walks of life? Will the minister tell the House how

June 30, 1981
Oral Questions
many hours, or even minutes, it will take before the strike costs the people of Canada more than it would have cost the government to settle this past weekend?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me assure the House that members opposite have no monopoly on concern for the people of Canada and the difficulties they will have in enduring this strike. The only monopoly most members opposite seem to have is one on complete and utter fiscal irresponsibility.

subtopic: UPGRADING OF RAW MATERIALS AND RESOURCES BEFORE EXPORTATION
UPGRADING OF RAW MATERIALS AND RESOURCES BEFORE EXPORTATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Trade. As the minister is no doubt aware, Canada's share of world trade dropped by some 33 per cent during the decade of the 1970s, particularly in manufacturing finished products. Is it the intention of the government to bring in a new trade policy which would require greater upgrading of raw materials and resources before they leave this country, thus providing jobs in Canada instead of elsewhere in the world?

subtopic: UPGRADING OF RAW MATERIALS AND RESOURCES BEFORE EXPORTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the hon. member on his new responsibility with respect to trade. I look forward to working with him in the coming days in this regard.
It has been a policy of the Government of Canada to put greater emphasis on the further processing of our raw materials, and in particular on the sale of end products to other countries. Once the hon. member has a detailed look at our trade figures he will find that although our end products decreased last year, partially manufactured products increased substantially. This also has a substantial labour component. Last year was the first time in the last nine years that there was a surplus in the combination of Canadian end products and partially manufactured products.

subtopic: RESTRICTIONS ON CANADIAN SUBSIDIARIES OF FOREIGN MANUFACTURERS
RESTRICTIONS ON CANADIAN SUBSIDIARIES OF FOREIGN MANUFACTURERS
speechtext: Despite what the minister has said, Madam Speaker, last year in this country, in terms of finished products, we had a deficit of some $18 billion. I am sure the minster is also aware that many Canadian subsidiaries of foreign manufacturers are prohibited by their head offices from entering into world markets. What effort is being made to free them from this restriction, on behalf of Canada?

subtopic: RESTRICTIONS ON CANADIAN SUBSIDIARIES OF FOREIGN MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I ask the hon. member to look in further detail, as I
responded in my first reply, at partially manufactured products. He is right with respect to the deficit in end products, but in partially manufactured products which, for example, include lumber from western Canada for houses in Japan, and is not classified as an end product because we do not ship the houses, and newsprint which is classified as a partially manufactured product yet we do not ship newspapers, if he looks at the whole broad spectrum of partially manufactured products rather than end products, he will see that we had a surplus rather than a deficit.
With regard to the second part of the hon. member's question concerning branch plants of foreign multinationals, my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, is putting a great deal of emphasis on World product mandating. We have several excellent examples in Canada of branch plants of foreign based multinationals doing an excellent job in the export of products manufactured in Canada.

subsubtopic: REPORTED PHASING-OUT OF VIA RAIL PASSENGER ROUTES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Transport. It deals with the apparent announcement yesterday that certain VIA passenger services are to be abandoned or phased out, including the Barrie-Toronto run, Stouffville-Toronto run, and the Havelock-Peterborough-Toronto run. Is it true that the phasing out of those three lines is under consideration and that it is anticipated that the lines will be turned over to the Ontario government to run as part of their GO train service? If that is the intention of the federal government, has it notified the Ontario government that such an action is planned?

subsubtopic: REPORTED PHASING-OUT OF VIA RAIL PASSENGER ROUTES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the decision of cabinet has not been made on this subject. As we are reviewing everything that concerns VIA, hon. members should understand that what the hon. member mentions may be part of the review now taking place. I would like the House to understand immediately that the purpose of this minister and cabinet is to save VIA, to break the vicious circle which now exists under which we have constantly escalating operational deficits for VIA. Because of a number of restraints we are not capable of improving the capital budget of VIA so that this vicious circle can be broken and VIA can begin to be a much more modern and able passenger transportation company than it has been up until now.

Madam Speaker, I hope the Minister of Transport will tell the House why he seems to have such a double standard. It was only on June 26 that he agreed to a $40 million special federal subsidy to re-equip commuter train services in the Montreal area. Yet he tells us in the name of restraint he intends to cut back on VIA and
June 30, 1981

intends presumably to put more costs on the Ontario government, a government that he has already reneged on paying $30 million which was pledged by his predecessor in that portfolio. Why does the minister have this double standard whereby in some cases cabinet decisions have been arrived at to give a $40 million subsidy to help the commuter to and from work in Montreal, but there is no such subsidy for those in the Toronto area?

Madam Speaker, it has been the policy of the government since 1975, and even before that, that commuter services, because of the nature of their operations, are a municipal-provincial responsibility, not a federal one. This was confirmed by decisions of the CTC in a number of instances. What has happened in Montreal is a recognition of that fact. Because these lines in the city of Montreal have been neglected for a number of years, the Government of Canada decided to make a contribution, as it did in Toronto in 1967.
I would also point out that $30 million of that $80 million that is going to urban transportation in Montreal is given under the UTAP program, which is a decision that the Quebec government has made, allocating that amount of money to this particular purpose. Any province can do that. However, Ontario has not decided to do that.

MEASURES TO AID MOVEMENT OF INCREASED EXPORTS OF GRAIN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. Considering the prospect of rail rationing in western Canada, and given the fact that Canada's grain carrying fleet will be reduced by some 50 per cent by 1985 due to the retirement of some 7,000 boxcars because of age, what program or steps is the federal government taking to ensure that adequate rolling stock will be available to move the anticipated export shipments of 30 million tonnes by 1985? Specifically, why has the minister's department not yet accepted the proposal of the grain transport authority, endorsed by the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat, Board, to acquire 1,300 new units of rolling stock on an annual basis for the next five years?

subtopic: MEASURES TO AID MOVEMENT OF INCREASED EXPORTS OF GRAIN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is the view of the government based on a number of studies, some of them by the grain transport co-ordinator, that there is no need for more hopper cars this year. The lead time for ordering hopper cars is, I understand, six months. The government will have plenty of time to order needed hopper cars for the next year, if that assessment is made.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON USE OF RAILWAY SERVICES
GOVERNMENT POLICY ON USE OF RAILWAY SERVICES
speechtext:
There seems to be some inconsistency, Madam Speaker. A spokesman for the government suggested there will be rationing in western Canada of the utilization of the rail system. I will direct this question to the Prime Minister. Was the government leader in
Oral Questions
the other place expressing government policy when he said this past weekend that the federal government plans to ration western Canadian rail space with a system of allotments for exports from the west? That was stated by the Hon. Senator Ray Perrault. He indicated that by 1985 it will be necessary to ration rail space in western Canada. Will the Prime Minister advise if that is an expression of government policy? If so, it is a classic cop out.
How will the government have sufficient capacity to move the anticipated 70 per cent increase in rail tonnage over the next five years and meet the anticipated export target of 30 million tonnes of grain by the year 1985?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON USE OF RAILWAY SERVICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the leader of the government in the Senate was simply expressing the view that unless something is done in due time, this is the situation that will exist in 1985. That is what he said. There would be a possibility of rationing of the main line. He was projecting to the future what will happen if decisions are not made, but those decisions will of course be made.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF ROBERTSHAW STUDY OF CHILD FATALITIES CAUSED BY PARENTAL NEGLECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. On April 21 in this House the minister assured the people of Canada that the Robertshaw study on child abuse, which was looking into problems which lead to the deaths of up to 200 children per year, was completed. The minister further stated that:
I am happy to say that I shall publish her report on child abuse.
Since there appears to be some discrepancy as to the status of this report and seeing as no report has yet been published, could the minister inform the House whether it is the study of the issue that has been completed, or the final written report, including recommendations, or had Mrs. Robertshaw been taken off the project before she had completed the real work she set out to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: STATUS OF ROBERTSHAW STUDY OF CHILD FATALITIES CAUSED BY PARENTAL NEGLECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the study conducted by Mrs. Corinne Robertshaw is of a judicial nature and deals with child welfare legislation especially the provisions to protect children against violent abuse. We could ot/iously continue our investigation. However we considered this study could serve as a good working paper. As I said several weeks ago, we would publish whatever we could with the approval of our contacts. I should have a report within a few hours on the extent of what can be made public, but I know that to protect

June 30, 1981
Oral Questions
the children, several of our contacts would not allow us to publish the entire report. The work was completed in a satisfactory way a few days ago so that it will now be up to the parties concerned, in particular the provinces, to decide what they will do next.

Madam Speaker, the reason the minister has had difficulty getting some of this material released for publication is that people do not want to do anything which would preclude the completion of the final written report. It is the written report which the minister promised us on April 21. Therefore I repeat my questions to the minister. Has Corinne Robertshaw written a final report? If not, why not? If so, where is it? What is the mandate of the responsibility centre for children which the minister also mentioned on April 21 about which there has been no press release nor any details? When will the minister make good on her commitment to publish the written report and tell us something more about this responsibility centre for children that she was so rhetorical about two months ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member is confusing several issues here. The Robertshaw study was conducted under the auspices of my department by this researcher with the assistance of another department. The study was supposed to last a couple of months but it finally stretched into twice that, if not three times. I think it has progressed to the point where we could publish the recommendations. As I just said to the hon. member, I should be advised within a couple of hours on the substance of the matter because I think some informers did not want their testimonies to be published. We will publish what we can. There is no need for the hon. member to cause a scandal or a controversy over something which is not that.

subsubtopic: F-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT-ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR QUEBEC
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Supply and Services about the situation regarding the F-18 fighter aircraft. According to press reports over the past few days and especially yesterday, the F-18 fighters would be by-passing Quebec, and three quarters of the economic fall-outs which had been promised to Quebec would practically disappear. Could the minister indicate what actually are the figures involved in these economic fall-outs from the F-18 contract, and whether to date the terms of the agreement have been fully met by McDonnell Douglas? Also, in case of non-compliance with these terms by the corporation, are penalties provided for under this contract?

subsubtopic: F-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT-ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR QUEBEC
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I dare hope McDonnell Douglas will comply with all the terms of this contract. I should like to point out to the hon. member that when the contract was signed, McDonnell Douglas indicated that some $1,570 million in economic fall-outs would go to the province of Quebec. I must add that my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and I were both in Bromont yesterday for the official opening of a new vane and blade manufacturing plant which should generate some $600 million in economic activities. The original agreement called for only $60 million in respect to this plant, and the corporation has already promised to invest $97 million; moreover, nearly $500 million in economic activities will be generated between now and 1995. While there, we also announced a contract between McDonnell Douglas and Canadair which should yield nearly $92 million in economic fall-out. There is also a new digital rolling mill which has been promised, so that the benefits to date exceed the expectations of the original contract with the corporation.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION RESPECTING CAST SHIPPING GROUP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport concerning the involvement of the Canadian National Railway Company in marine transportation. The minister has been warned that CNR's involvement in the Cast shipping group would create problems in Canadian ports. The minister knows that the U.S. Congress is considering a law to control marine carriers which transport U.S. cargo through Canadian ports, and he has caused diplomatic representations to be made to the U.S. Congress.
The minister must know that this law was motivated by Cast's predatory pricing policies, by its support from the Government of Canada, and by the CNR through financial assistance, through sweetheart deals in the port of Montreal, and in other ways. How will the minister explain his position to the U.S. Congress, and how will he explain this government's position to this House?

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION RESPECTING CAST SHIPPING GROUP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think my hon. friend is exaggerating unnecessarily. This attempt by the Congress in the United States to pass a bill affecting transportation of U.S. goods into Canada is one that comes forward at regular intervals in the United States. The Department of External Affairs is aware of the situation, and it has sent a note through the embassy to the Congress on this subject. Congressmen, who are quite intelligent as are members of Parliament, will sooner or later understand that this is not a good line to take, because on the west coast the
June 30, 1981

situation is exactly the opposite. On the west coast Canadian shippers make greater use of U.S. ports than vice versa. Therefore, we have a balancing act, and I am quite sure that reason will prevail in the House of Representatives.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to know that the minister thinks I am exaggerating, because Mr. Richard Lidinsky, in testifying before a committee of the U.S. Congress, referred to the Cast shipping group as a James Bond-type of operation and he asked Congress to pass this law. Does the minister not think, in view of the allegations that have been made in the United States, in view of the fact that the Dart shipping group moved from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal because of the Cast-CN connection, that it is time to call, under the provisions of the National Transportation Act, a general inquiry into shipping traffic through east coast ports so that all of those concerned in the shipping industry in Canada will have an opportunity to present their views? This time Mr. Bandine may be willing to testify, because he was not willing to testify in the hearing held in Halifax by the CTC concerning Dart and the CPR.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR GENERAL INQUIRY INTO EAST COAST SHIPPING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sorry but I do not have before me the curriculum vitae of the gentleman whom the hon. member mentioned a moment ago. But the information I have is that he is working for one of the ports on the east coast, which makes him somewhat of a party in the debate.
On the subject of the relationship between Halifax and Montreal and other ports on the east coast, I thought there was a good airing of the subject in Halifax a few days ago, and I am quite sure there will be other opportunities.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ALL-INCLUSIVE SPORTS BETTING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport. It deals with my question to the minister of last Friday, which reads in part, as reported in Hansard at page 10983:
Is the minister telling us that neither his department nor any other department of government has been considering sports betting?
The minister responded, in part, as follows:
We do not contemplate any such scheme as the hon. member has mentioned.
1 would suggest that the minister was either ignorant of matters relating to his jurisdiction or he was misleading this House, because I have here a sample of a betting ticket produced by the federal government which would bet on 15 hockey games, called Sports Select. This is not Loto Select nor the computerized games. Therefore I ask the minister to set aside his sarcasm of last Friday and try to give an honest and intelligent answer on this matter.
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ALL-INCLUSIVE SPORTS BETTING PROGRAM

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I knew that the Prime Minister does not always tell the truth, but now the disease is spreading to the minister as well.

Madam Speaker, on Friday the minister categorically denied-

speechtext: Order, please. If the hon. member has a supplementary he can ask it right now.

If the penguins across the way would give me an opportunity, I will. On Friday the minister categorically denied the government was even considering sports betting, and I quoted "sports betting". Now there is a sample ticket which the government has produced for hockey sports betting.
Oh, oh!

If the government is not considering this type of sports betting, which on Friday the minister categorically denied, what is the minister considering? What is the program for future gambling operations of the government when the Liberal government prior to this one assured this House that it would not go beyond the Montreal Olympic betting operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member may remember that last week I told him he

June 30, 1981

speechtext: What the hon. member says is totally incorrect.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition seems to be having trouble, or a fit, or something. Perhaps he can let me answer the question for the hon. member. The hon. member says that the government said it would never go beyond paying off the Olympics in Montreal. It never said any such thing. Furthermore-
You were not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: Furthermore, Madam Speaker, long after that the government was still in Loto Canada. The party opposite was involved in Loto Canada when it formed the government, so it would have been in breach as well. This government is looking at various options. I have not even had the privilege to see the form that the hon. member is looking at, but I will be happy to examine it if he would like to send it over.
Madam Speaker, let us go back to the Minister of Transport and some more gambling with safety and lives.
Oh, oh!
Shame!

Since the railroads and the chemical and dangerous goods manufacturers are weeping and wailing and pleading high costs before the Canadian Transport Commission on the implementation of the Grange report, and since the bible of the Liberal party, the Toronto Star, says that the required changes in rail safety regulations should be made regardless of the cost, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport if he will call upon the CTC to order the railroads to speed up substantially their installation of hot box detectors on all the main and secondary freight and passenger rail lines in Canada?

Madam Speaker, the CTC has already done that. While the hearings are going on, and I understand that they are coming to a conclusion now, the CTC has issued an order telling CP to implement in the next year the plan that they had for 1985, if my memory serves me well.
The Grange Commission made a number of recommendations. I have already reported to the House on that subject.
Nine of them are presently being implemented, and six are before the CTC.
I received a letter recently from a distinguished minister of the government of Saskatchewan, telling me that there must be a happy medium between preoccupation with safety, which obviously is important, and the economic health of the country. I suggest that this would be good reading for the hon. member for Regina West.

Madam Speaker, the distinguished minister in Saskatchewan knows how slowly this Minister of Transport, and previous ones, and the CTC have moved, and that this could affect the movement of commodities out of western Canada very seriously.
Since the incident at Sundridge, Ontario, occurred on a CNR line from Toronto to North Bay, which has no hot box detectors on it, I hope the minister will see to it that the CTC looks into that matter.

Madam Speaker, the purpose is obviously to reduce the number of accidents we are getting, as the hon. member says. But I was looking yesterday at another accident in White River, Ontario, where the train was equipped with roller bearings. This proves that, with or without roller bearings, there will be accidents. My old friend is right, however, that an effort should be made to reduce the number of accidents. This was the purpose of the Grange report, and it is the purpose of the hearing before the CTC now.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR OF ROYAL BOTANICAL GARDENS IN HAMILTON, ONT.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. The minister should know that Canadians are now the world leaders in ornamental horticulture, and Canadian gardens located in several parts of Canada, including Montreal, Victoria and Niagara, are viewed by travellers as superior to most in the world. Will the minister tell the House why a work permit was approved for the Royal Botanical Gardens in Hamilton to allow it to appoint a person other than a Canadian to the post of director?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister took the position in the Stratford Festival instance that he had to be shown that a proper and extensive search was made to make certain that Canadians would have first opportunity to take that kind of job. subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF MARIAN STASTNY TO CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. According to Austrian authorities there are 10,000 refugees from eastern Europe in Vienna, many of whom want to come to Canada, have applied for permission, and have to wait for long periods of time before their applications are even considered. Given those facts, I should like to ask the minister how it is possible and by whom it was arranged that Marian Stastny could go to Vienna and within a few hours of visiting the Canadian Embassy, be on a plane coming to Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Loyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ADMISSION OF MARIAN STASTNY TO CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, we have
Point of Order-Mr. Mazankowski a special category of immigration for those who come from Eastern Europe. We call it the self-exiled class. They are given very minimal requirements to meet, basically health and security checks. We have substantially increased the levels we set for that class this year, up to 4,000, which is an increase of
1,000	over the previous year. In this case the application by Marian Stastny was under that classification. He was given no privileges different from anybody else, with one exception. Under those circumstances we afforded him the same kind of protection we afford anybody in those circumstances; if we cannot guarantee security in Austria they are given the chance to come here and then go through landing procedures here in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at this particular point I should like to explain to the House the reasons for having posted the items under supplementary estimates (B), as I have done, which appear on the order paper. Now that the government has tabled bills to cover all those particular items, it is not my intention to press with that notice. However, I wish to raise a point of procedure which I think requires clarification.
Under the rules, hon. members have always been given the right to post a particular item for an expression of opinion by the House. I recall, as a member of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization at the time, that hon. members would be allowed to post any particular part of the spending program for approval by the House.
What has happened is that somehow or other a form of notice of opposition was taken by the table. That requires 24 hours of notice prior to the deadline of consideration, but automatically, even though the government has not acted on it, a motion in positive terms is put on the order paper.
That motion oftentimes includes a much greater sum than the one of the hon. member wishes to oppose. For instance, in the Senate it could be broken down, yet the total amount is put forward. This puts the House in a dilemma in that while one might be in favour of certain items, that on which one wants an expression of opinion is swallowed by the whole. I fail to see why this should be allowed in so far as an expression of opinion by hon. members is concerned.
I put forward the proposition that those items in supplementary estimates (B) should not be concurred in. That is the motion which, 1 suggest to the Chair, should be taken by the Table and put to the membership; rather than the Table itself

June 30, 1981
Estimates
converting it into an affirmative motion and saying that these items should be concurred in.
This is the point I wish to raise. I would wish a clarification on it in due course, but I now formally withdraw all the postings of the estimates in supplementary estimates (B) which appear in my name.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES
speechtext:
1 can give clarification to the hon. member. The procedure is to allow a member to raise an objection about certain items in the estimates which have been dealt with item by item in committee. When the estimates come again before the House, the member is allowed to raise an objection to one or several of the items in the estimates. This is what the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has done. He raised a number of objections to several items in the estimates which the Table transformed into a positive motion precisely to allow the House to express an opinion on the particular objections of the hon. member.
If I am correct-and I stand to be corrected-these objections were about different items, but they were not lumped into one motion. In the end there will be an all encompassing motion to accept the estimates. If the procedure is followed, the House will have had a chance to express an opinion on each and every objection raised by the hon. member.
This is the clarification I offer to the hon. member. I hope it satisfies him. I take note of his desire to withdraw these objections which he posted with the Table.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: that Bill C-77, respecting oil conservation and the substitution for oil of other energy sources be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
Let us hear from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his invitation to address the House for a few minutes on this bill entitled an act respecting oil conservation and the substitution for oil of other energy sources. Bill C-77 provides for the implementation of the Canada oil substitution program which is a very important element for our National Energy Program.
The National Energy Program pointed out that Canada's problem is not really a shortage of energy but that, as a matter of fact, Canada is a net exporter of energy to the tune of roughly $3 billion every year.
We have a problem in connection with oil supply and particularly, we must deal with our pattern of energy consumption which relies on oil and is producing, in effect, a growing dependence on oil imports. Obviously we should do everything we can to increase oil supply in this country by new discoveries all over Canada. The fact is, however, that all experts agree that it will take a few years before an increase in supply can be relied upon. In fact, it was forecast, before the National Energy Program, that we would see our imports increase substantially until at least 1985-86 until new sources of supply from the tar sands plants and new discoveries in Canada lands, would become available.
The Government of Canada decided that in those circumstances it was essential that steps be taken to dramatically shift energy sources for Canadians away from oil and toward those forms of energy that we have in abundance, such as gas, electricity, renewable energy generally, and coal.
Related to this, obviously, we also have, in the National Energy Program, a very dynamic conservation program encouraging Canadians to save energy. Later this afternoon one of my colleagues will address the question of conservation, particularly through the CHIP and HIP programs for home insulation in this country that have been effective for a few years.
When talking about the Canada oil substitution program, we refer to our off-oil conversion program for residential and industrial heating. This program represents our most important single lever for rapid adjustment and it constitutes the cornerstone of our drive toward independence from the world oil market within this decade.
The goal of the Canadian Oil Substitution Program is to reduce the use of oil in the non-transportation sector, that is in the residential, commercial and industrial sectors, to 10 per cent of energy use by 1990. I am happy to report to the House that this is a goal that is universally accepted. The provinces and industry agree that it can be done with the co-operation and careful management of all parties concerned. But there is a long way to go. Oil now accounts for 37 per cent of the energy for heating homes in Canada.
[ Translation]
For example, in my native province, Quebec, the percentage is even higher than 37 per cent which is the national average. If I remember well, some 61 per cent of Quebec homes are oil heated. Therefore, we are aiming high since we are striving to
June 30, 1981

reduce that percentage in Quebec, for example, from 61 to 10 per cent during the coming decade.

For the whole of Canada, getting to 10 per cent means we need more than two million conversions of heating systems in this country over the next decade. As a matter of fact, our goal is to achieve this objective early in the decade rather than late in the decade. This will mean a large investment in all parts of Canada. It will mean the creation of new firms, new jobs for thousands of Canadians, and I am happy to see that many firms, organizations and individuals are arranging their affairs to take advantage of this development in the energy sector in Canada.
Clearly, however, this objective will not be reached without an assistance program because the capital cost of conversion will otherwise discourage many Canadians from making the shift. We have therefore set up a grant program that will make this feasible and will quickly pay back the investment for both sides through a reduced compensation payment on imported oil by the national government and through lower heating bills for individual Canadians.

In fact, COSP which we are asking the House to approve formally this afternoon under Bill C-77 meets various needs throughout Canada, since it will help Canadians through substantial grants to change their type of energy consumption and to convert from heating oil to other forms of energy, either gas, electricity, coal, wood or any other form of renewable energy. In addition, the government has defined the allowable costs in a very general way to make sure that the heating systems will be efficient and safe when Canadians will be converting their system to a form of energy other than oil.
The grant provided under this act and COSP will cover half of the conversion costs up to $800, and the eligible conversions will include the conversion of an oil fired heating unit to another type of fuel, converting it for instance into a gas burning unit. Also, the program will cover the costs of replacing an oil fired heating unit with a gas or electricity heating unit. Finally, the program will allow the addition of a back-up system, such as a wood stove or an electric heat pump, which would reduce the level of oil consumption in the current heating unit by at least 50 per cent.
We have put together a very flexible scheme which offers consumers a freedom of choice and, for all practical purposes, makes it possible for them to transform fully and completely their heating units if they want to, or to transform their units gradually, on condition that their converted systems uses at least 50 per cent less heating oil.
In effect this $800 grant is designed primarily to assist the home owner in meeting the up-front costs of converting. It will also be helpful to smaller commercial establishments. As far as

centrally heated apartment buildings are concerned, a formula applies which will provide conversion grants of up to $5,500 per building, depending on the number of units.
Finally, for larger commercial and industrial buildings, we have come to the conclusion that the major incentive to convert will be the growing difference between the prices of oil and gas provided under the National Energy Program. As a matter of fact, we have foreseen that the wedge, or the spread, between the price of oil and gas, will increase appreciably over the coming decade. Already that spread is substantial indeed. In fact, in the past without grants or subsidies, we have seen that the price wedge has already led to hundreds of major conversions wherever natural gas service is available. Because of the nature of the country, the nature of the services that are available in Canada and the types of energy that are available here, we have had to develop a flexible program in order to respond to the availability of non-oil energy sources across the country. For the main part, I would say that the renewable portion of COSP applies across the country and that there are no differences to speak of while the gas and electrical components are tailored to regional availability and to provincial preferences.
We have had extensive discussions with the provinces during the last few months about this particular program. We have made every effort to tailor the program to answer the concerns of the various provincial governments. We have been led to introduce certain restrictions at the request of some provincial governments, taking into account their particular situations with regard to energy supply.
If we go across the country, I would say first that Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and the Territories where electricity is generated from oil and where natural gas service is many years away, COSP takes the form of a conversion program to the various renewable energy sources and, second, it takes the form of assistance to upgrade insulation and improve heating efficiency. What we have in those provinces is a program derived from COSP that we call super CHIP, which is the $800 available in the other provinces for conversion to natural gas, wood or electricity. In those provinces it becomes a program to convert to renewable resources. Also it can be used to add on to the existing CHIP program so that people can at least be assured they will have a very generous scheme for home insulation. Thereby we will be in a position to encourage conservation much more significantly in those provinces compared to any other strategy. In effect, in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and the Territories we already have energy experts in the field who will recommend in detail improvements that home owners can make to reduce fuel consumption.
In the Maritime provinces, the National Energy Program provides for a fund of up to $500 million to assist with the construction of the natural gas pipeline to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Also if I can jump to the other side of the country, it will provide, if necessary, support for the construction of a gas pipeline to Vancouver Island so that COSP can
