[ Translation]
In Quebec, the program has already been announced. It is already being implemented with respect to the substitution for oil of all sources of renewable energy as well as natural gas. The public is aware of the nature of this program. It provides any single family with grants of up to $800, but such grants may come as high as $5,500 in the case of multiple-unit housing. The problem which remains outstanding has to do with the conversion to electricity. I was surprised to learn from a number of my colleagues in the House that people calling Hydro-Quebec are told that the government of Canada alone is responsible for the fact that grants for conversion to electricity are still not available and that they must contact their federal member of Parliament to settle that problem. I want to say very clearly to the people of Quebec that if they are given that type of information over the telephone by people from Hydro-Quebec, it is definitely unfounded. In fact, in the past few weeks I have had a number of conversations with my colleague the Quebec energy minister, and I was expecting an answer from the Quebec cabinet on June 3 last.
For all sorts of reasons the Quebec government have found it impossible to reach a conclusion on that issue until these past few days. I am scheduled to meet very soon with my Quebec counterpart, Mr. Duhaime, with a view to settling that question as soon as possible. I certainly regret the very protracted delays we had to experience in Quebec as a result of that situation, and I hope that as a result of my forthcoming meeting with Mr. Duhaime we will be in a position to announce to the people of Quebec that without any further delay they will become eligible for the $800 grant to convert to electricity. Be that as it may, I must point out that since the program was first made public, the government of Canada has been ready and willing to make those conversions to electricity eligible for the grant and that we are waiting for the Quebec government to give us the green light to launch the program efficiently for all Quebec residents who are anxious to change their heating system to electricity.
I entertain every hope that we will reach agreement very rapidly and, in that case, the people of Quebec will be able to benefit fully and without any restrictions from all aspects of the Canadian Oil Substitution Program.
I would now like to deal with the other provinces west of Quebec-
First, in Ontario and Manitoba where virtually all alternatives to oil are widely available, COSP will apply fully. It will have the enthusiastic co-operation of the gas utilities and, we anticipate of electric utilities including the several hundred independent public utility companies in Ontario which are being invited to participate in the program delivery.
We have had many meetings and discussions with those utilities and we have had discussions with the provincial governments concerned. I am happy to report that we have received the full co-operation of everyone. In those two provinces, this program is already fully effective. I invite the public to make full use of that program.
I have already talked about Manitoba. In the other prairie provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, it is a fact that they are largely off oil. Alberta is very much the model province for COSP. Alberta has already reduced its residential use of oil to below 10 per cent. That is an achievement which is indeed remarkable, when we think of the oil that the province has and also the gas. I am happy to pay tribute to the foresight of consecutive administrations in that province which have pushed actively for the consumption of natural gas. In that province, by a very large margin, oil consumption for residential, commercial and industrial purposes is very much below that in other provinces.
The program of conversion to gas and electricity is not operating at this time in Saskatchewan, I regret, in view of the provincial government's preference for an alternative more appropriate to the province's circumstances. At the present time there are discussions between the two governments. I hope we will be able to reach an early agreement so that the people of Saskatchewan can have the full benefit of this program like people in most other provinces in Canada.
COSP will apply in Alberta for conversions to gas and renewables. There remains a considerable potential for rural conversions to gas in the northern part of Alberta.
In British Columbia the COSP program will help extend the use of natural gas on the mainland and eventually on Vancouver Island in line with provincial government priorities. That provincial government has resisted the extension of the program to conversion to electricity. Therefore, the program will essentially be applicable to conversions to natural gas.
A separate component of COSP is being developed in discussions with each province to provide funds over the 1980s toward the expansion of distribution systems for gas, electricity and renewable energy resources. This, too, will be a flexible instrument directly tailored to provincial and regional needs and priorities. However, this program will not become effective during the current fiscal year. It will not begin until the 1982-83 fiscal year at the earliest.
After having said a few words about the extent of the program and how it covers the country, I would like to say something about the delivery agents for this program. The gas and electric utilities play a very important role in the delivery of the gas and electric part of COSP. They are the channel for application forms and program material and a source of information on program rules and the conversion alternatives available. Once home owners have converted, they return completed application forms to the utilities concerned, either hydro or the gas utilities. These forms can then be verified and forward to the federal government which will issue the grants directly to those who have converted to gas or electricity.
June 30, 1981

With regard to the renewable and conservation portions of the COSP program, that will be delivered on behalf of my department by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This will be done following the two-stage application process adapted by the Canadian Home Insulation Program, CHIP. When there is a request for an application form, the form is sent out, completed and processed on the basis of the application form. This allows for much better control of the grant process. There will first be the COSP application request card and then a personalized application information package. This will ensure that we will be able to reduce to a minimum the possibility of a misuse of funds provided under this program.
The delivery agents, whether the utilities or CMHC, will establish that conversions have in fact taken place, that they are eligible under the rules and that invoices support the work actually done and the equipment actually installed. These are important tasks which help prevent abuse and ensure efficiency in the operation of COSP. The delivery agents are reimbursed for performing these steps. We have reached agreements with the various utilities whereby we pay them a certain amount for each application form that is processed. Therefore, the utilities, whether hydro or gas utilities, will not lose money as a result of processing these forms.
Furthermore, there will be an important link between the gas and electric components of the program on the one hand, and the delivery system for the renewables component of COSP on the other. There will be an automatic computer check of applications against gas and electric applications to ensure that duplicate grants are not paid at any address unless permitted by COSP rules.
To prevent abuse of public funds and to ensure that individuals make informed decisions about converting, the distribution of application forms is handled exclusively by utilities for gas and electricity and by CMHC for renewables. This can be explained further in the context of the various steps being taken to provide good advice to applicants.
Before concluding, I would like to say a few words about the question of advice to applicants.
[ Translation]
I indicated quite clearly that our program would give Canadians wishing to convert their oil heating system the widest possible choice. Of course this flexibility is somewhat limited in some provinces because of decisions taken by the provinces themselves or because some sources of energy, like natural gas, are simply not available. But it is up to the applicant to decide when conversion will take place and what source of energy he will convert to, as well as what type of equipment he would purchase. I want to make it positively clear that the decision is up to the individual.
Naturally, there are various factors that come into play, for instance the individual's personal preferences but the government will do nothing to influence the individual in choosing one solution rather than another. However, under this program the government wants to encourage Canadians to consider
Oil Substitution and Conservation carefully all the alternatives and to ask the relevant questions. In fact, there is a whole range of services available to individuals considering conversion. First there are the brochures on the Canada Oil Substitution Program, which recommend that homes be better insulated, that overly large heating systems be avoided and that several estimates on the work to be done be obtained; other pamphlets have been prepared on each alternative energy source eligible under the oil substitution program; and, finally, various publications of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources of Canada deal with heating efficiency and energy savings. In addition, the advisory service of Ener-Save provides free inspection by mail to determine insulation needs and a free telephone information service is also placed at the disposal of Canadians. Finally, my department has opened regional offices in each province and both territories to provide information about the program; in every case, the telephone numbers may be dialed toll free.
I just about forgot to mention that my department has Enercentre stands in shopping centres and other public places throughout the country to provide information on energy programs, including the Canada Oil Substitution Program. Finally, public utilities, that is both the hydro companies and the natural gas companies, for instance, are other major sources of information on the criteria of the program and conversions to gas or electricity.
The objective of this whole set of sources of material and information is to allow citizens to proceed to the transformation of their heating systems away from oil and to allow them to make their decisions concerning their applications for grants with adequate information at hand. Vast experience suggests that if application forms for the grant program proliferate, the risk of fraud and uninformed decision-making increases.
In conclusion, COSP is a major, essential part of the National Energy Program. It goes directly to the problem of oil imports with a solution that is based on the use of cheaper and more abundant domestic alternatives. The program will have a raid pay-off in terms of lower heating bills. COSP will also benefit the suppliers of the alternative fuels. It will benefit manufacturers of gas and electrical equipment, wood burning systems and solar systems. It will benefit retailers of oil equipment and systems. It will benefit thousands of private contractors who will make these installations all over the country. It will spur the development of technology and the introduction of more efficient heating equipment. COSP will have a payoff for the country in reduced dependence on expensive oil imports and in growing energy securities. COSP in that sense is a global and team effort of people all over the country, and I urge the House to give this program its enthusiastic support.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side are pleased to be able to look at Bill C-77 which encompasses COSP. I just want to draw to your atten-

June 30, 1981
Oil Substitution and Conservation
tion that this bill was not available to anyone on this side, at least not to myself, until two o'clock.
The minister in his opening remarks on the Canadian oil substitution program talked about the need to become energy self-sufficient, or self-sufficient in oil, and to remove the people of Canada from the use of oil as an energy product without affecting the use of oil in transportation.
At the outset I would like to say that we on this side have some questions, and we will get to those I am sure when we are in Committee of the Whole on this bill. The one thing I should like to point out to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, is that devising a program encompassing all of Canada is not like devising a program that encompasses a smaller country. Our nation, with its different climatic changes, different energy supplies, different natural resources in each region, is a very vast country, and it is almost impossible to apply a universal program, as, I am sure the minister and his officials have found out. I am sure the minister and his officials have worked hard to try to make the program apply universally with the same effect on every citizen in our country. This has nothing to do really with provincial governments or the lack of co-operation. This relates to the nature of our country.
We feel there is one area in which the minister could find an additional 120,000 barrels of oil every day in Canada, if he would put his mind to it. He could do so by coming to an agreement with the province of Alberta regarding oil cutbacks in Canada. He would then find an additional 120,000 barrels of oil in Canada he does not have to import from overseas suppliers.
When we look at the problems different provinces have had with the application of the universal program of COSP, we should briefly touch upon situation which exists in the two western provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
We in Saskatchewan are being denied 50 per cent of this program. At the request of the provincial government, and I am sure this is not the fault of the federal government, natural gas and electrical power should not be included in this grant program. Therefore, all we have available in Saskatchewan is renewable grants or grants in respect of wood. I find that very strange because in my province we rely on electricity for a considerable amount of our heating. I guess this is because in my province a lot of natural gas is imported from our neighbouring province of Alberta and used to generate electricity. That to me is a very ridiculous program, particularly when we consider the vast hydro resources that exist in northern Saskatchewan. I will later be asking the minister several questions that I am sure he posed to the provincial government of Saskatchewan, and I hope he will be able to supply some answers.
The need for energy self-sufficiency within Canada is not something new that the Liberal party which forms this government has come upon recently. On December 6, 1973 the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a statement to the effect that the main priority of his government at that time was to reach energy self-sufficiency by 1980. I believe he said the end of the decade, and I presume that meant 1980. I would
doubt that the statement we have heard that we will become energy self-sufficient by 1990 has any more credibility than the previous statement made in 1973.
I would like to put forward a supposition, and later ask the minister to comment. As regards the methodology used to reach energy self-sufficiency by 1990, I presume officials built a supply curve. I assume the minister's department theorized, added a few tar sands plants and a few renewable resources and built a theoretical supply curve. Then, I presume, the people in the minister's department said: we know in the year 1990 we have to cross this curve because the government's policy is self-sufficiency by that time. By building a mythical supply curve and taking the year 1990 as the crossover point, I assume the government arrived at the decision that Canada would have energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
I hope the methodology of that supply curve will be made available to hon. members on this side of the House at a later date or, hopefully, in the Committee of the Whole. There have been some problems with government involvement and with CHIP in the recent past. One of those problems has been in relation to the amount of time people eligible for those grants have had to wait for them. I hope the minister will act to reduce this burden because interest costs are now running at 21 per cent or 22 per cent. These people deserve to receive their grants quickly. Perhaps rather than sending grants from a central location, several offices could be established across Canada. This would enable people to receive their grants much sooner.
Offices have been established by the minister's department in Edmonton and Calgary to handle the Canadian oil substitution program. In both cities I doubt very much if there are 500 people who are presently using oil. The off-oil program in those two cities does not keep the offices very busy. If the minister checks with the people staffing those offices, he will find that they are having a very relaxing time because there is just not much demand in those two cities.
As the minister stated, there is a vast rural natural gas program in Alberta. We in Saskatchewan do not have that. However, there are reserves of natural gas in Saskatchewan which could enable us to have natural gas available throughout rural Saskatchewan comparable to the situation in the province of Alberta, if only the federal-provincial atmosphere were a little more favourable. In this instance I think I can point particularly to the provincial government.
Six months ago the premiers of the prairie provinces briefly discussed an electric power grid. It was proposed that a joint network of power grids be run from Manitoba through Saskatchewan and into Alberta. In this case I find it strange that the provincial governments appear to be waiting for funding from the federal government in 1982 or sometime in 1983. I find that not to be much to my liking. As much as I feel sometimes that the minister is responsible for some things, I think in this case the minister is not to blame. The premiers in this case do not have the ability to get together and run a
June 30, 1981

power grid which would serve all the people of the prairie provinces.
While hon. members on this side welcome the Canadian oil substitution program, we do not find it to be a program which will be applied equally to the people of Canada. We find that regrettable. It is another example of trying to establish a universal program for a country as diverse as ours. We look forward to some of the answers we will receive from the minister when we go into Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to indicate to the minister that I think it is obvious to everyone that the direction of the program makes good sense. I do not think anyone looking at the problems of Canada and the problems of the world today in terms of the availability of oil could quarrel with a series of programs which ultimately will reduce our dependence on the petroleum companies of this nation and of the world.
On balance I think the program is supportable. However, I want to raise a few concerns. No one really believes we can continue forever to depend on oil. I once said in the House- and I believe it as strongly today as I did the day I said it- that I hate to think of the value of the last drop of oil when we finally find it. I am always concerned that we are putting, even yet, too much of our time and effort into the seeking of that elusive last drop of oil rather than spending more time, effort and money on the development of those alternatives which are renewable and will last through a number of generations.
I am never happy with the predictions of the oil companies.
I can recall not so many years ago when we were told quite clearly by the oil companies that we had sufficient oil to meet our demand needs for the foreseeable future, whatever that was-for a great time into the future, at least. It only became apparent when the price of oil started to rise in the world markets that the oil companies were either hoodwinking us, unable to tell accurately what the supply situation really was, or taking advantage of a situation which had arisen.
I think the future rests almost entirely on conservation. The off-oil policy is a good policy. In the short run, we have to utilize the existing alternatives, but I think the long-term future lies almost entirely in energy sources which to this point in time are probably little used and may even be quite costly.
It is toward cost that I want to address my remarks because, frankly, I am concerned. I have a nagging worry about the future. We are encouraging people to move from oil to electricity, natural gas and other energy sources, and quite rightly so. However, as people move to other energy sources, we have to keep in mind that the ownership of the energy source to which people are moving remains very much within the ambit of responsibility of the very same people who currently own the oil. I am worried about the fact that we may well be moving people to those alternatives and that the end result may be price gouging.
I raise that because if anyone were to ask me today where he should put his money, if he has any, I would advise him to put it into banking or other related institutions because they seem
Oil Substitution and Conservation to be making a buck or two these days. I would advise him to put it into energy, and particularly oil.
A statement is written up in today's newspapers indicating Imperial Oil is not prepared to go ahead with the Cold Lake project unless it is guaranteed a 20 per cent return on its investment. As we look at the rest of the economy, we must ask ourselves what kind of people are these people who insist on 20 per cent profit when any number of small businesses is going out of business today and when all other sectors, with the exception of banking and related concerns, are facing very serious profit crunches. What kind of people are they who, because they happen to have a product which is essential to the well-being of Canadians, will hold Canadians to ransom and demand from Canadians a guaranteed profit level in this wonderful free enterprise system in which they live? It made me stop and think when I read about it because I realized, as I looked at Imperial Oil with all its diversification, that it is entirely possible we are asking people to move from using oil to alternative sources of energy at a considerable cost to themselves and the public purse, and they will still end up buying from Imperial Oil. Imperial Oil will still be extracting this usurious amount of profit from these unsuspecting souls ten years from now.
Therefore, I want to suggest to the minister that while it is important, which I cannot deny, that we move away from dependence on oil, if only because it is a finite resource, and we encourage conservation and the utilization of renewable resources, we must at the same time put in place mechanisms to monitor both the availability, price and the profit flow from this absolutely essential commodity. I do not want to see us have another combines investigation of the new companies which are going to be set up to meet the energy requirements ten or 15 years from now and then discover, when that investigation is complete, that during this period of concern over availability of energy, these selfsame companies who ripped us off-I think a lot of people would admit that has happened over the last ten or 15 years to the tune of many billions of dollars-are simply able to rip us off even more by virtue of investing most of that money in alternative resources which are not monitored or controlled.
I do not want to see people put in the position of converting from one source to another only to find the cost of providing for their energy needs is no longer controlled or monitored, and they are going to find themselves paying exorbitant amounts of money to these companies which operate today in what they see is a very lucrative area. They will demand from those consumers that same 20 per cent profit level they are demanding in today's newspaper.
Who is going to bear the cost of what we are doing today? The taxpayer will at every level. It does not matter whether it is directly through their taxes or the price of energy, they are going to carry that cost. We have the direct costs, the cost of replacement of heating units, in some cases the cooking units. That is a direct cost, and the government through this program

June 30, 1981
Oil Substitution and Conservation
has made available sums of money to compensate for it, but of course that is money raised through taxes of one kind or another. Then there are the indirect costs the consumer will have to bear. Those are costs the major companies in the field are able to write off against taxes they should be paying. It is the cost of subsidies, write-offs and tax concessions. These companies demand on the one hand a 20 per cent return on investment, and on the other hand they write off against their taxes costs of exploration for research and development into alternative energy sources. So in every single instance, all the way down the line, the cost is going to be borne by the consumer.
Now I say to the minister in all fairness, I really do worry about the fact we do not yet have a handle on the way the major energy corporations are able to reach into the consumers' pockets. We do not have a way of monitoring fairly and accurately the degree to which they are able, year after year, to take from the unsuspecting and, in many cases, unprotected consumer. Of course, they would argue that, having taken for years when there was a sufficient supply of energy, as the supply begins to dwindle they need to get even more because, after all, it is in short supply. It then becomes a commodity with a much greater value because there is not nearly as much of it.
So I want to suggest to the minister that while I support the thrust of what he is doing and while I recognize that in both the long and short term it is preferable we move from the heavy reliance we have on oil to reliance on renewable resources, I want to be sure the government is going to put in place mechanisms to monitor the price to the consumer in order to guarantee there cannot be the kind of obvious rip-off that Imperial Oil is attempting to perpetrate on the Canadian public by their demand for ever higher prices in order to get a 20 per cent return.
I realize the government may not be prepared to admit to Imperial Oil that they can have a 20 per cent return. I can appreciate it may well be the government does not support Imperial Oil in that demand, but what worries me is that this company, the largest of the large, with untold reserves of capital, which for many years has had a privileged position in Canadian society and has been able to recover all of its costs by way of tax write-offs and concessions, and which has had to spend little in the way of after-tax dollars in the development of its enterprise, seems to think that a 20 per cent level is a fair return. They seem to think because they are in the field of energy it is all right to expect 20 per cent, given of course that the Canadian taxpayers have already put $40 million into the Cold Lake project.
Good investment.

It could be a good investment, nobody is going to deny that, provided it does not permit Imperial Oil to then demand a pound of flesh from the consumers.
I want therefore to suggest to the minister that concurrent with this legislation, with these expenditures and initiatives, a way to guarantee protection for the Canadian consumer must
be put quickly in place. As we encourage people to move from the use of oil to other resources, we must recognize those resources will in most instances be in the private sector and we must put in place a means of assuring that the kind of unwarranted, unacceptable and unjustifiable rip-off which has taken place over many years by the multinational oil companies is put to an end. Also we should ensure that no measure can be taken by any of the producers of the new energy sources which will allow them to do to us in Canada what the oil companies have been able to do over the course of the last 15 or 20 years.
I do not want to see old age pensioners putting most if not all of their expendable life savings into making this changeover. I do not want them to suddenly discover that they are paying two or three times what they were paying previously, simply because the persons who are producing the new energy source think they have a captive market. We must be very cautious about that. I have seen it happen too many times; once they have consumers in a vice-like grip, where they have already made the investment and can no longer afford to reinvest, the price begins to escalate. Of course the end result is that people are forced to cut back in many other areas.
There are large numbers of families across the country who can ill-afford to make any further cuts in their standard of living in order to satisfy the greed of energy producers in this country or in any other country. I am not talking so much about gas because I realize there is the National Energy Board before which hearings will be conducted and prices established. Also I realize that, in the area of electricity, there are procedures, at least in Ontario and, I suspect, in other provinces where hearings are to be held, to determine the price structure and price level. I am talking about the newer more innovative methods, the renewable resources we are hoping will become a major part of the Canadian energy scene. Sometime between now and next year we should quickly put in place a method to guarantee that what Imperial Esso is attempting to do cannot be done by anyone else entering the energy field in Canada in the future.
I want the minister to say to Imperial Esso that the 20 per cent is too damned much, that this is not a game we are in. No one can expect to get a 20 per cent profit margin guaranteed by the public of Canada. Imperial Esso cannot expect this, nor can anyone else. If Esso wants to continue to have access to our oil resource, the oil of the public of Canada, then it better act in a responsible way and recognize that every penny of the cost will ultimately be borne by the consumer and the taxpayer.
No matter how Esso juggles its figures, it cannot possibly justify what it is requesting in economically hard times such as the ones we are experiencing now. It is a situation which, I suspect, we will be in for some time to come. The minister should put in place some way to ensure that we will never again be left at the mercy of greed. This is what it is. I would have thought by now that companies operating in the country
June 30, 1981

would have realized that greed cannot be tolerated, that there is no place for it. We cannot afford them if that is what they expect us to do. We would much rather do it ourselves than have it done for us and done to us at the same time.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to say how much I appreciate the minister's outline of the bill. Rarely in recent years have we had from him this type of comprehensive yet objective account of his legislation. I think this should be pointed out.
Oil Substitution and Conservation
I do not think there is any question that the House in general understands and supports the purpose of the oil substitution program, but I would like to raise a series of small points, if I may, in the hope that in the performance of the bill under the minister's administration we can improve it somewhat.
My first point has already been covered by the minister, namely, that we require a separate type of program with each province. I am conscious of the fact that he dealt very lightly with the province of Saskatchewan which did not have much reason for barring those people of Saskatchewan from the federal program who had converted to electricity or natural gas. I will say no more about that. It is up to the people of Saskatchewan to skin their own shunks. I suppose they will do it within the next year or so.
My second point concerns the philosophy of the program, and I want to end my remarks with a question. It is a good philosophy to get as many people in the low technology systems as possible to move away from the consumption of oil. It is particularly good, if the alternative is cheaper not only than the present price of oil but the future price as well.
I am somewhat concerned about the fact that there is so much pressure to convert to natural gas or to electricity. I do not believe they will meet the test of low-cost energy for the people of Canada. When I look at the interest rates and the capital intensity of the structure of moving with electricity and the production of electricity, I know that these interest rates will show up in high prices for electricity for many years to come. Be that as it may, certain things can be done that were not specifically mentioned by the minister in his remarks today which I believe come under this bill.
The bill tries to provide encouragement through incentives in the form of a grant to get people to convert from oil to any type of energy which is generally available and, hopefully, cheaper. Will the minister tell the committee whether a heat pump will be acceptable under this grant system?
Before the minister rises, I want to point out the fact that all across Canada, but particularly in rural areas, almost every farmer has a well, a dug-out or some form of water nearby with which he can heat his house. Many people have lawns in front of their houses and gardens at the back on which there is enough heat stored in the form of solar heat which will heat a house during the winter. This has been done for 50 or 60 years; but the heat must be converted into a form which can be used by interposing a heat pump. A heat pump is not a new device. It has been used by the housewives of our country for some 60 years in the form of refrigerators which take the heat out of food and pump it onto the floor. That same type of apparatus can take heat out of air, out of the ground and out of water and put it into the house. At the present time this method is much cheaper than the heat obtained from oil or natural gas. I would like to ask the minister whether a heat pump will come under the $800 provision in this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first, I would like to thank the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain for his kind words. I would like to take this opportunity to stress his well-known interest in this field for many years.
I would like to answer the hon. member very quickly. Heat pumps will be eligible for conversion grants. Obviously, this depends on the agreements we have with the various provinces. We do not yet have an agreement with Saskatchewan, and in Nova Scotia this matter is still being negotiated. However, in all the other provinces heat pumps are eligible for the grant. I hope that since discussions have started again with the government of Saskatchewan, this will become the case in that province. Although heat pumps represent a large investment it is our view that they also imply very substantial savings in terms of energy consumption and particularly of converting from oil.

I would like to put this thought forward to the minister, Mr. Chairman. I hope that when he is negotiating with the province of Saskatchewan, which above all other provinces needs this type of item in the arsenal for fighting home heating costs, he will consider what I have to say. With the research that has been done in the last two years I feel I can say fairly accurately- and the minister can verify this through the National Research Council-that if you are heating your home out of air, the co-efficient of performance is about 1.6 to one. I know that is the Canadian Standards Association level for Ontario, but it also applies in Saskatchewan. If you are heating your home with water or from the ground, as long as you put your heat exchanger below the frost line or below the ice in the water source-in the case of wells that is always open-you can obtain a co-efficient of performance of close to four to one. Translated into dollars and cents, that means if you tried to heat your home out of the air around your home over the year, a dollar spent for electricity to run the electric motor, which runs the compressor in the heat pump, will give you $1.60 worth of heat. This, it is a good deal. But if you heat your home with a heat pump where your heat is obtained from a constant source, such as the water in a river under the ice of the water in a dug-out or a well underneath the ice, and if you have built a storage thank, you obtain a co-efficient of performance of approximately four to one. At present prices, that means $1.00 of electricity gives you $4 worth of heat. That is a tremendous saving. Of course, that saving increases if oil prices rise.
Something to remember about a heat pump-that is where the difficulty might arise for the minister-is that in those provinces if you put a heat pump into your home, you are required to have a back-up furnace, either an electric one or an oil or gas furnace. If you put the heat pump beside the existing furnace and use the same fans and electrical system to operate it, your installation ban be at a minimum cost. I hope the minister will suggest to his officials and to the provinces when he is dealing with them that when they deal with applications for heat pumps, it will not be a requirement to remove your old furnace when putting in a heat pump. If the heat pump will
provide you with over 50 per cent of the heat supply for your house, you should not be required to remove your old furnace. I would like to ask the minister whether this is looked after in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The comments made by the hon. member are confirmed-it would be quite a challenge to match the hon. member's own expertise in this field. I would like to tell the hon. member that there is no requirement under the federal rules for the existing system to be removed if one wishes to instal a heat pump. As a matter of fact, we quite understand that an existing system can very well be maintained. The only requirement is that the new system which is to be installed must replace at least 50 per cent of the oil consumption which occurred before installation. As the hon. member has explained, that would be achieved by the installation of a heat pump.
I understand that some utility companies in certain provinces insist on the previous system being kept. For instance, the government of Quebec is considering an arrangement whereby it would allow conversion to electricity only in so far as the previous system would still be maintained as a back-up with the possibility of converting to oil or gas later on. I do not expect there would be great difficulty in this regard. It is a matter in which the provinces could have an influence in terms of their powers over provincial utilities. As far as we are concerned, we certainly do not intend to make any such requirement, that is, we see no problem with keeping the back-up system in operation.

I appreciate very much what the minister has just said. It has been my experience that no matter how well intentioned your programs are, they can sometimes be messed up, to use a polite word, in the translations, and through the regulations in the various types of programs.
I have several other questions. I do not want to take up too much time but I would like to offer some suggestions to the minister. I do not think my suggestions can be covered at the present time under this bill. They might very well be covered in the next version of the bill. I am talking about the fact that one of the ways we can save money and the use of oil is by utilizing in our heating systems passive solar energy. For instance, I would like to use one example. The province of Saskatchewan has developed a very convenient and simple technique for storing heat from passive solar energy through the use of sodium sulphate mixed with peat. Without going into all the fancy details, a person can build a storage facility for a small home which would cost only $1,000. That facility can store the surplus heat provided by solar energy through ordinary windows. That is why it is called "passive". You can store the heat from days when the sun is shining and bring that heat back into your home during the night.
The research work in this field which has been done by the province of Saskatchewan shows that the technique is long-lasting. Incidentally, the first place where this apparatus is being sold is in Ottawa. It is very simple for a person to handle
June 30, 1981

this apparatus. It is just like the ice pack that you take along on a trip in the summer to keep things cold. You can buy any number of bags. They can be set along your windows to collect enough heat to heat a house, according to the experimental work which has been carried out. All the time that the sun is shining and the room is hotter than 70 degrees in the sunshine hours, heat is being collected into these bags. The minute the room temperature drops below 70 degrees, the bags begin to pass out the heat they have collected. This is a simple type of technology. If one were to spend money on that and to add to one's passive heat it would be a substitution for oil. I know it is not possible the way the bill reads now. I wish the minister would keep in mind that if anyone can offer a proven technique to reduce the use of oil, it should be included in the bill, just as a stove is. I just thought I would throw it to the minister and hope he will keep it in mind.
I want to move on to some more realistic ideas, Mr. Chairman. We waste a tremendous amount of heat in our homes through the gray water that goes out into the sewers. By gray water I mean water from washing machines, the baths and sinks, water which is dirty and so is called gray water. Usually it goes out still containing heat. Some research has been done by the University of Saskatchewan which shows that by spending about $100 for a heat transfer system, the heat could be extracted from the water and transferred to a water heater. This is only legal in Saskatchewan, however. The minister could approach the other provinces with a view to having them change their health regulations to allow individual householders to direct the gray water to a tank where the heat could be extracted and then transferred to the hot water tank. This would save 50 per cent of the cost of heating water in the household, which at present is roughly $200 per year. This is a type of proposal that I think we could sneak into the bill as a way of getting individuals to adopt methods which would save a substantial amount of oil.
There is one thing that I hope the minister will take up with the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman. The bill provides for an $800 incentive taxable grant. In the propane legislation it is $400. Other legislation gives a two-year accelerated write-off to anyone who uses renewable energy hardware. I have already written to the Minister of Finance with a suggestion. I wonder if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources could support me in saying that in order to be fair in applying this to all Canadians, this proposal, which only applies to those income taxpayers who have capital cost allowances under their form of income tax, should be extended to individuals who live in towns and country homes, who do not qualify for the capital cost allowances that farmers and businessmen qualify for.
If those millions of people who live in town or city homes had access to the same type of tax incentive as the farmer or businessman who has the advantage of the capital cost allowance provision, it would be a break for them. Officials in the Department of Finance are familiar with the tax credit concept. If this could be applied, it would be a tremendous incentive to the people who have to go into the more extensive,
Oil Substitution and Conservation
expensive types of conversion. A heat pump for a small home will cost about $2,000 or $2,500 and close to $3,000 including installation. The incentive to the taxpayer, if he could get the same deal as the person who was claiming a capital cost allowance, would be tremendous.
It is estimated in the United States that in the next ten years there will be a heat pump in almost every home, and certainly in every building. Billions of dollars worth of business will be generated in providing these heat pumps for heating and cooling. There is roughly $15 billion worth of business for Canada in the next 15 years as well. I think the individual who puts up money for the conversions in order to save oil, natural gas and electricity, is probably doing more for his country than can be done in any other way and without great expense to the government. What the government can do to get people to convert from oil to other energy is nothing compared to what 24 million Canadians could do who are willing to convert, first of all, because it is cheaper, second, because it is cleaner, and third, because it is renewable. We can push this concept of conversion from oil to natural gas and electricity by using the knowledge which is available to us.
I am not going to ask a question, Mr. Chairman. I want to conclude by congratulating the minister again for bringing this legislation forward and allowing us to ask him some questions. I hope he will consider the suggestion that I have made to improve the legislation and make it available to all Canadians. If so, we could achieve this conversion from oil to other energies more rapidly than this bill can by itself.

Mr. Chairman, before asking one or two specific questions, I want to make some brief remarks and indicate that although I agree with the direction of this bill, I have some misgivings. First of all, I want to touch briefly on the universality of the program, second, on the incentives for conversion and third, on incentives for the supply and distribution of a specific form of energy.
I was involved in the rural natural gas program in Alberta which gave monetary incentives for supply and distribution rather than for conversion. The provincial government made sure that gas was available, through co-operatives, that it could be tapped by users and that it paid, to a large degree, the supply-cost to the user. In some cases the subsidy amounted to $2,900 per user and in other cases it was less.
It effectively guaranteed that the price of the energy supplied would not exceed the price of other energy forms. Before anyone connected to a natural gas system, he had some guarantee that the price of his energy would be lower than other forms of energy in the foreseeable future.
I shall ask the minister whether in the negotiations on energy pricing in Canada, he is going to guarantee to all persons who hook up to natural gas, that the price will be 65 per cent or 75 per cent of the price of oil. He might tuck that in the back of his mind so that he can answer it later.
The incentive for moving in this direction is a saving on the consumption of oil, but it is also really a saving on the federal government's subsidy for imported oil. That is the real incen-

June 30, 1981
Oil Substitution and Conservation tive. When I look at the chart showing the growth of oil consumption and natural gas consumption in Canada, they show that over the period 1962-1976, the consumption of natural gas increased three and a half times while the consumption of oil increased twice. 1 do not think the figures have changed too much since 1976 when the residential area was using 265,000 barrels of oil a day, the commercial sector was using 100,000 barrels of oil a day and the industrial sector was using 220,000 barrels of oil a day. From what the minister has said, I gather he is looking for a saving of something in the order of 100,000 barrels to 150,000 barrels of oil usage in Canada. Therefore, there is a saving in federal government subsidies for imported oil because the government is subsidizing the imported oil going to the Atlantic and eastern provinces.
I do not think there are many of us who do not realize that the energy utilization in Canada will shift to gaseous fuels and electricity, or to solar energy and heat pumps, as the former speaker indicated, but primarily for a period in the future it will be gaseous fuels and electricity. Gaseous fuels are natural ones. They can be transported through pipelines with a very high Btu content. This includes natural gas and synthetic gas from coal and biomass, as well as hydrogen produced basically from electricity, as was indicated in the report of the committee.
But if one is going to move to provide incentives for conversion to the natural gas area or to the gaseous fuel area and electricity, surely one must look at the cost of supply of these systems. One must look at the cost of the availability as well as the distribution of that fuel for residential use. I suggest that if you reduce the cost of supply and distribution greatly, because the end user's costs are always three or four times the cost of the fuel itself, by the time you factor in the cost of supply and distribution, particularly with the interest rates we have now of more than 20 per cent, the real incentives to the users are not necessarily the end cost of the fuel itself but massive subsidization of the supply and distribution system.
It bothers me that there is no crash program in existence in Canada today, I mean a crash program to distribute the enormous quantities of gaseous fuels that we have available in Canada to all areas of our country. We must not only supply it to an area but distribute it to the people, and the costs of distribution are high. I would have thought that the federal government, besides coming forward with a conversion program, because conversion is done automatically when the supply is there and the costs are right, would undertake, on an emergency basis, a program of supply of gaseous fuels literally to most of the nation. Second, I would have thought the federal government would provide the necessary subsidization of the distribution system so the costs of supplying it can be brought to the users at reasonable rates.
I have two questions for the minister. Does he have under consideration any grants or subsidization whatever in relation
to the cost of supply and the cost of distribution of gaseous fuels as well as electricity?
I was involved in the western grid system and the availability of hydro power. The distribution of electricity throughout the west, was enormous costly. Does the minister have a subsequent program of supply and distribution for gaseous fuels as well as for electricity for residential conversion from oil to gas? Second, can the minister guarantee a price Structure to the people who convert from oil to natural gas so that the cost of natural gas will be consistently lower than the equivalent cost of oil on a Btu basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the first question asked by the hon. member, I indicated in my earlier remarks that we have already set aside a fund of $500 million to help construct a gas pipeline to the maritimes. Part of that money may also be available to help the completion of a gas pipeline to Vancouver Island so that all regions in this country will be provided with a gas trunk line system.
As to the second element on the help to expand the distribution systems, we have also provided funds that will become available next year at the earliest for the expansion of distribution systems in areas where it is uneconomical to do so at this time. We would not seek general subsidization for the expansion of gas lines or electricity lines anywhere in any province. It would be in places only where expansion would imply massive substitution away from oil in those areas where it is marginally uneconomical at the present time. A fund of this type would be available for this purpose.
As far as the second question raised by the hon. member is concerned, I am having discussions with the producing provinces on a new oil and gas agreement at the moment. I can tell him that all the producing provinces agree that there should be a significant differential in favour of gas compared to oil. This is very much a basic element of our own policy. I can say that as far as the national government is concerned and as far as the governments of the producing provinces are concerned, we are all in agreement that we should maintain an appreciable differential in favour of natural gas versus oil for the foreseeable future.
We are talking about an agreement lasting several years. I have no doubt that such an agreement, if it were arrived at, would ensure that any investment citizens would make in favour of natural gas at the expense of oil would be a very good one for those who convert. Obviously I cannot guarantee the kind of provincial taxes which would be imposed on the various forms of energy in the future. But again, all my conversations with the various provincial governments indicate they recognize that preference should be given to natural gas as opposed to oil for residential, commercial and industrial purposes.
I think citizens of Canada can, with a great deal of confidence, proceed to investment in natural gas, knowing that over the years the advantages of natural gas compared to oil will be substantial.
June 30, 1981

In the National Energy Program we have a proposal which will take the differential down as low as 65 per cent, I think perhaps even lower than that, but I do not know what it will be once our negotiations are concluded in particular with the government of Alberta but 1 can assure the hon. member that all governments agree that this is the direction in which we should proceed.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's answer. He has answered as forthrightly as he could at this time. However, he spoke rather glowingly about conversion from oil to natural gas. Have any studies been made by his departmental officials to suggest strongly that conversion to electricity may have the same benefits as conversion to natural gas in the future? I think the minister has indicated that with appropriate subsidy for supply and distribution of natural gas and some guarantees on pricing, he would not be fooling people in terms of conversion, that they will in fact have an advantage in years to come. I again ask what guarantees, analyses and studies has the department done to supply some sort of assurance to people converting to electricity from oil as against conversion to natural gas?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some studies have been done, but the situation varies considerably from province to province. We do not have a complete study that would constitute a report on the national situation in this regard. This type of work has traditionally been done at the provincial level by the provincial departments of energy in so far as they control the gas utilities and hydro. We have not been able to get price forecasts for electricity for years to come from some provinces. That information is not readily available with regard to all the provinces. However, I will be happy to inquire from my officials which provinces can give us that type of forecast.
Canadians all over the country can assume that when electricity originates from sources other than oil, it will be cheaper to switch to electricity than use oil. That is a kind of general statement. As to whether it would be advantageous to switch to natural gas rather than electricity, that matter will have to be examined in every province. I suggest that individuals check with the gas utility, if there is one in the area, and hydro, compare the cost estimates and arrive at their own conclusions. As we know, individuals make decisions not only on pure cost factors but on other features as well. If the two services are available, I suggest that individuals obtain quotations and proposals from both utilities and then make their choice.

Mr. Chairman, I want to raise another question; the minister did allude to it. Canadian citizens should be cautioned to some degree about conversion to electricity for residential heating. I hope that the literature to be put out does not put the major emphasis on conversion to electricity because it may appear acceptable and appropriate in the short term. In the longer term, for example a period of five to ten years, it may not be as attractive as is being suggested at this time by some of the officials in government.
Oil Substitution and Conservation

Mr. Chairman, I have a question with regard to Clause 5, development assistance. I will put a hypothetical situation so that I can get this cleared up quickly. Am I to understand that if one of the existing oil companies, which has already put into its price structure the requirement for the possibility of investment in other than oil, decides to acquire an existing company or go into discovery, development, production, transportation or storage of other than oil, natural gas or electricity, it would be eligible for grants, loans, or financial assistance guarantees from the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, Clause 5 is permissive. It provides for administrative discretion in the approval of grants. It is a matter the minister will have to determine on the basis of each application, taking into consideration the validity of the project, the cost benefit, the discovery that could be made and the ability of the company concerned to carry the cost on its own. Obviously we would have to treat differently an individual who has a bright idea, would like to develop it and only has a few dollars and an application from Imperial Oil. This is something the minister and the administration will have to take into account when the various proposals come forward. This is done all the time with the various grants or schemes in operation in the different departments of government.

May I just pursue this a little further. The bill refers to "discover, develop or produce". To produce is a little more difficult. The ones that worry me are acquire, transport, store or make available for use. If a person wanted to acquire an existing alternative energy source other than oil, electricity and natural gas, or wanted to acquire the transportation system, for example the trucks to move it, or wanted to set up a storage facility for future use-make available for use is ambiguous but that is beside the point-is it possible to come to the government under those circumstances for a grant, loan or guarantee to enable him to do this?
What sort of criteria will be established to enable people to understand whether it is even worth their while to make application? I can imagine any number of people looking around the world for a variety of different enterprises they could acquire, taking on a transportation system and using government funds to get the trucks or setting up two or three metal sheds for storage purposes at public expense. Is that what the minister is talking about?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Obviously one can think of the most ridiculous situations and say it would be terrible if grants were made in such cases. One can go through the various pieces of legislation and imagine a rather silly administration doing silly things. Clause 5 is of a general nature. It refers to grants to persons, governments or institutions. The legal draftsmen tried to ensure that there were not too many restrictions with regard to the applications for grants.
It may be that a municipality wishes to acquire a certain heating source or discovery from abroad and requires a grant either to acquire or transport it. It may represent a possible breakthrough. The municipality might need some help in order

June 30, 1981
Oil Substitution and Conservation to achieve that purpose. The government would have to examine whether that heating source represented something new, whether the cost benefit was appreciable and whether the institution applying for the grant was in need of it. I repeat, these are very general provisions. We will have to look at them on the basis of the various applications.

I know the minister will forgive me for my dubious and doubting ways. However, the whole thing is so ambiguous as to allow people to drive trucks through it. I really do not understand it. All it does is say that the government will be able to give away public funds in whatever way it sees fit to anyone it wants to at any time as long as the people are not in the business of providing oil, natural gas or electricity and can claim to be in a business related in one way or another to the provision of other than those three energy sources. That whole clause is permissive, and "permissive" does not describe it.
The record of the government in terms of its handouts is part of the reason that Parliament and the public of Canada seriously question the fiscal responsiveness of governments here and everywhere else. Will there be regulations? I do not see any indication that there will be. I have certainly looked at the clauses here. There is no reference in Clause 5 to regulations, although Clause 3 specifically makes reference to them. Can the minister help me on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I may be able to speed this up and help my friend on this subject. If he reads the beginning of Clause 5 he will see it says "Subject to any regulations made under this Act and in accordance with such terms and conditions, if any, as the Treasury Board may specify". You end up having both regulations and specific conditions the Treasury Board puts out before approving a request for funds for this particular purpose. These are all public conditions and regulations that the applicants would know. There are considerable restrictions there. In addition the funds voted for this would be controlled by Parliament through the estimates. There would be considerable control over the spending both by the government and by Parliament.
As far as the general comments of the hon. member are concerned, this clause provides the necessary discretion to provide grants for development assistance in new forms of energy. Unless my hon. friend wants the minister to come before Parliament every time and have a vote on every grant, I am afraid he has to be reconciled with living with administrative discretion.

My final point is that Clause 5 says: "Subject to any regulations" which are made. That does not require that there be any. It says: "Subject... to such terms and conditions, if any, as the Treasury Board may specify". That does not mean there will be any. I just want to suggest that it has been my experience, limited here though extensive elsewhere, that the legislative process is certainly no guarantee there will be fiscal responsibility. The minister knows as well as I that we
are forever approving expenditures long after they have been made.

Mr. Chairman, first I would like to commend the minister for introducing a bill which will make it possible for many Canadian families to save energy. However, I wonder if any study has been made. Already in our metropolitan area and in many other areas of Canada there is a very heavy demand for contractors to convert systems from oil to gas and it would seem that those contractors are charging over and above normal prices. I am therefore wondering whether your department has studied the possibility of training additional contractors so that there will be a more realistic balance between supply and demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I think the hon. member is raising a very important and most interesting point. The Department of Manpower and Immigration is responsible for training manpower and the required staff in Canada. I think that my department as such does not have to assume that responsibility. However, inasmuch as citizens are involved, I would advise and encourage them not to decide on the strength of a single offer but so seek tenders from two or three different contractors; they will find out that quite often there are significant differences between tenders. One would be well advised to call tenders and not rely on only one bid.

Mr. Chairman, I have a second question. I wonder whether the minister is now having discussions with his Quebec counterpart since Quebec does not have an 8 per cent tax on heating oil, which it must import from foreign countries. On the other hand, local energy sources such as electricity and natural gas are taxed at 8 per cent. This seems to me very illogical because the consumer will thus lose a good part, or 8 per cent, of what he will save by converting his heating system. I therefore wonder whether the minister has had discussions with provincial officials in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Once again, I recognize that the hon. member for Duvernay is raising an extremely important question related to the Quebec tax policy. What he said is quite right, and it is unfortunate that there should be this additional tax of 8 per cent on natural gas, for instance, in Quebec.
Before the recent elections in Quebec, Mr. Berube, the former Minister of Energy, had stated that the Quebec government planned on doing away with this tax when gas is more widely used in Quebec. I have already raised this question and I intend to raise it again with the new Quebec Energy Minister, Mr. Duhaime, and I hope that he will succeed in convincing the Quebec Finance Minister to do away with this tax, which is really counterproductive as concerns the total energy policy that we are trying to implement. It is indeed somewhat ridiculous to impose a tax on electricity and gas when it is the demand for oil that we want to reduce, especially in Quebec. I
June 30, 1981

am glad that the hon. member has raised this point, and I thank him for his support in this regard and I can assure him that I shall raise the issue once again with the Quebec government.

Mr. Chairman, in fairness to the minister I think I should ask him the question I said I would in my reply to his opening remarks. The province of Saskatchewan has accepted less than 50 per cent of this COSP program. We in Saskatchewan are well aware that we have a Crown corporation which distributes natural gas and electricity to the people of Saskatchewan and which made, in my opinion, an unconscionable profit last year. Would the minister explain to the House why the government of Saskatchewan asked that the people of that province be deprived of over 50 per cent of the benefits of this program, which is, indeed, a national program?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should first of all like to thank the hon. member for his comments on the bill at first reading stage. I want to tell him that I was somewhat surprised to hear from the government of Saskatchewan that the reason it was not favourable to the extension of the COSP program to the additional 50 per cent was that in the case of electricity the cost of extending electrical service would be too high as far as it was concerned. That government felt it did not want to incur the additional cost that bringing additional electrical service to the citizens of the province would entail.
As far as natural gas is concerned, the government felt there was already a reasonably large coverage of gas consumption in Saskatchewan and it did not feel the need for an additional subsidy. I understand now that the government is reviewing its decision. I would not like to misrepresent that situation. There are discussions taking place at the present time, again between officials of the Government of Canada and the government of Saskatchewan, and I do hope, indeed, that the people of Saskatchewan will have the same global access to the program as the people of other provinces.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, it is correct that we had planned these debates with the three half-hour speeches at second reading. We just assumed that the time in Committee of the Whole would be very limited. I am a little reluctant to cut the Committee of the Whole debate out altogether. I would even go for 20-minute speeches at second reading if we could have 10 or 15 minutes in Committee of the Whole. Perhaps we could just leave it to common sense. If in Committee of the Whole there are some obvious points of order or questions which should be raised, we could govern ourselves accordingly. However, on the basis that we are not ruling out common sense, we agree.
