speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we took our dinner recess there was some discussion about the merits of brevity. I shall accordingly attempt to be brief in my comments on Bill C-75.
This bill is intended to give further impetus to the energy conservation activities of the government. It also draws attention to that part of the National Energy Program which I regret has not received as much attention as the supply side; that is the need to conserve energy in Canada. We have had in place for some time a program intended to reduce the consumption of all forms of energy in the industrial sector. Earlier today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made reference to the co-operative arrangements that have been worked out between industry and government to give substance to our commitment to reduce the use of energy in the manufacturing industry in particular.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is one of the world's heaviest users of energy, but that of course is understandable given our vast territory, small population and an often hostile climate. Nevertheless, those factors should not be seen as an excuse for extravagance in our use of energy. Therefore, the conservation efforts embodied in the NEP, indeed in this bill, take on a special importance.
In addition to the industrial initiatives I mentioned, the NEP also envisages new rules regarding residential units which will be implemented as of tomorrow. Hon. members may have seen in the newspapers in the last few days the requirement that no new residential unit will receive federal assistance or guarantees if it is heated by oil, unless no other reasonable energy alternative exists.
In addition to the building requirements, we have embarked upon a program four years ago to promote better insulation in residences. CHIP is familiar to hon. members of the House; I need not dwell on it. It is the principal method of providing funds to encourage greater energy efficiency in our homes. Currently the residential sector accounts for approximately 15 per cent of primary oil use in Canada. We believe that through CHIP which was initiated in 1977 the federal government will be able to encourage a reduction in the consumption of oil and thereby contribute to our total goal of self-sufficiency by the end of this decade.
We have set some substantial targets for a reduction in home heating oil consumption. Home owners are clearly responding to the incentives we are providing through CHIP grants. In 1977 only 15,000 grants were made, whereas the estimate for 1980-81 is for a total of 500,000. This is clearly a
Canadian Home Insulation Program
substantial increase. Our present goal is to reduce by one-third the oil used for space heating in reinsulating residences.
The bill before us this evening draws attention to the benefits of the insulation program. It will also bring to mind, in the case of some hon. members and in the case of the public, the need to ensure that high standards are maintained in the insulation industry. The government has moved to ensure that certification becomes a basic feature of the total program. We have worked with the Canadian General Standards Board to develop a certification program for home insulation which will be in place on November 1 of this year. Indeed, after that date it will be mandatory for all contractors performing work under CHIP to be certified if they wish to continue in the industry. Equally, we have embarked upon a major program review to determine the extent to which CHIP has met its initial targets and to explore any modifications which may be needed in light of experience.
In our view, the program has proven to be a major success. It is an important feature of the total National Energy Program and indeed of the energy future of Canada. In terms of reducing Canada's demand for imported oil, the program has already reduced our needs by something over $2 billion.
I could continue with some more details about the program, but I hope my necessarily brief introduction is sufficient for a bill which I trust will win the immediate support of all hon. members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, if I had not
been in place tonight to listen to the introduction of the program more commonly known throughout Canada as CHIP in a somewhat cursory manner as a matter-of-fact program, I would not have believed it. I cannot believe that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) is so ill-informed that he is not prepared to address what is the major problem in Canada today.
Bill C-75 is a so-called act respecting the home insulation program for certain provinces. Surely the parliamentary secretary has experienced some degree of doubt in his riding about the workmanship and the legislation which have gone into the planning stages of CHIP. I do not think there is an area in my riding of Peterborough which has not corresponded with me on a weekly basis concerning the horrendous nightmare stories connected with the bureaucratic administration of this system of supplying moneys to people to insulate their homes. It is not being administered by the private sector. It is not being administered by the people who are best able to evolve a program which will work for the people, namely, the different regional areas across Canada.
Let me give some specific examples of where the program has created major problems not only in the riding of the parliamentary secretary but in many others. I have a letter from an insulator in Peterborough, George W. Scott, in which he refers to the total disregard and arrogance of the CHIP program. That is the subject. He had three cases where people received government cheques, cashed them and then claimed

June 30, 1981
Canadian Home Insulation Program they did not receive them. When he requested photocopies of the cheques, CHIP barefacedly refused, as was stated by an employee in the office in Montreal. This is the office one phones, the office with the magic 800 number. I defy hon. members of the House even to get a ring; usually the line is busy. He continues:
"It is against the law", and five minutes later as stated by Mrs. J. Barrette, "It is not a contractor program, and we do not have to help you".
He said that if this is the case it is time the idiotic government should find out from the business community what a serious mistake it is making in trying to administer what could best be administered at the provincial level.
1 do not suppose there are very many people in the Ottawa bureaucracy who understand the heating and energy problems in the provinces of the nation, and the same could be said for the provincial governments and in some cases the regional governments. Why does the government feel that it can administer, by instituting an 800 number, a program which will bring economical heat savings to the people of the nation?
Having said all that about the problems of the bureaucracy in administering the insulation program, the parliamentary secretary said tonight that we have a high consumption of energy in Canada because we have a hostile climate. I suggest to him that we have a hostile climate in Canada today because of the national energy policy and bills such as Bill C-75 which the government has endeavoured to bring into play through questionable means. This has already been evident to the House by the rulings of the Speaker.
Also the parliamentary secretary said that the government promotes better insulation. I challenge him to give evidence of that statement. 1 wonder whether the tens of thousands of people across Canada who used UFFI to insulate their homes feel that the government has given Canada better insulation and promoted better use of commodities in the conservation of energy. I will touch upon that a little later.
The parliamentary secretary said that we are moving toward self-sufficiency in energy by 1990. That statement follows on the heels of a statement made in the House tonight which suggests that we are high consumers of energy, by virtue of fact. What facts can the parliamentary secretary give us which would indicate that we have been moving toward self-sufficiency in the last year and a half to two years? What facts can he give us which indicate that we are not importing more oil from abroad, that we are not becoming more and more dependent on offshore sources for our energy needs than we were the year before? The importation of offshore oil is the principal cause of our national $14 billion deficit which this government is forecasting for the current fiscal year.
I question whether granting $500 per home owner for the current fiscal year will afford us, in the net result, greater independence from offshore oil supplies. This $500 per home owner totals in excess of $250 million, to use the hon. member's figures, if it were paid to some 500,000 home owners. In reality, if we did not have a hostile climate in Canada, if we
had not created a national energy policy which caused major divisions in our nation, we would be less dependent on offshore oil.
In discussing Bill C-75 1 would like to read into the record some of the concerns expressed by some of the standing committees of this House of Commons with regard to the legality of the process. Clause 7 of the bill before the House tonight reads:
The Canadian Home Insulation Regulations made by order in council PC 1981-1435 of May 28, 1981, shall be deemed for all purposes to have the same force and effect from July 1, 1981, as if they were made under the authority of this act.
In The Canada Gazette of June 10, 1981, under SOR/81-437 these regulations so appear under the Privy Council date of May 28, 1981. However, in a letter dated June 16, 1981, just six days after these regulations were published, from Mr. R. E. Fowler, senior counsel of the legal division of CMHC to Mr. G. C. Eglington, who is counsel for the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, there appears the following:
With regard to the need to expressly refer to paragraph 11 (2)(a) of the National Housing Act as the corporation's authority to prescribe standards, it is our belief that the needed change was not made. In this connection, I must say that notwithstanding a written request that we be shown a copy of the regulations well in advance of their submission for approval, the corporation was not shown a draft thereof. Our first opportunity to see the regulations occurred following submission of the regulations to Treasury Board, shortly before their approval by council. Our legal division was, as a result of a hasty review, able to secure a vitally needed change to the proposed regulations to rectify a problem affecting the ability of the corporation to carry out its functions under the program.
The failure to give effect to the standing joint committee's request is regretted.
I believe that an opportunity will soon arise to amend the regulations at which time the question of clarifying the reference to "standards" can be dealt with.
Notwithstanding the remarks of the senior legal counsel for CMHC that the failure to give effect to the standing joint committee's request is regretted, and that he was referring the letter from the standing committee to the director general of energy, mines and resources with the request that the department implement the committee's suggestion at the next opportunity, the irregularities which have lately been attached to this bill underline the inappropriate nature of the government's approach to legislation and regulatory reform.
As the preamble to the regulations, as published in The Canada Gazette for June 10, states, these amended regulations are made "pursuant to Department of Energy, Mines and Resources Vote 35, Main Estimates 1981-1982, as authorized by Appropriation Act No. 1, 1981-82." As my friend from Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) has pointed out, this vote is one of several which is not acceptable to the House as spending authority. Therefore, in so far as Bill C-75 accepts these regulations, through clause 7, which do not include changes recommended by the Standing Join Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, and endorsed by senior legal counsel for CMHC, I submit that clause 7 might not be sufficient authority to secure our satisfaction. It was not reintroduced into the House in a manner which reflects the 1980 recommendations of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments.
June 30, 1981

Having said all that, I would like to read into the record some examples which should not go unreported. One example which has already come to light regarding the rushed introduction of CHIP is the ill-considered means by which UFFI was approved. Another possible problem, as yet not addressed publicly, is the improper installation of conventional insulation. To quote from a Public Works Canada publication concerned with thermography, the use of special photographic techniques to assess the thermal efficiency of buildings:
Poor technical performance in buildings is common,... Recent investigations undertaken by Public Works Canada across Canada have revealed that defects in insulation placement, air tightness, and vapor control are common. They are often severe and cause high operating and maintenance costs. These inadequacies result in moisture accumulation on the inside surfaces of wall and roof construction. This reduces thermal effectiveness and in certain instances eventually causes material degradation.
Has the government considered performing a survey of houses insulated under CHIP with conventional insulation to determine whether the insulation methods endanger the structure of the house through moisture accumulation? If not, why not? Will the government be kind enough to table all correspondence and other forms of communication between the CDC, Lorcon or Rapco Foam and any of the departments concerned with home insulation, that is, CMHC, NRC, Public Works Canada and EMR? I have been led to believe that UFFI was given approval due to pressure brought by the CDC, which seems to control Rapco through Lorcon.
The government through the Department of Supply and Services, in the last few days has signed a contract with the consultants regarding a possible overhaul of CHIP. What problems are there with the program at present? How many different investigations or charges are under way by the RCMP? I would like to call for these papers to be supplied to members of the House of Commons.
When CHIP was originally announced in 1977, the government set a target of 70 per cent of all houses. Thus far the penetration rate in pre-1961 housing is markedly below the 70 per cent target. This raises doubts in my mind whether the 70 per cent can ever be reached.
A study by the Department of mines and energy in Nova Scotia showed that the average savings in houses insulated under HIP, which is now virtually the same as CHIP in the rest of Canada, was between 7 per cent and 11 per cent. What is the government going to do about this apparent failure? Does it even know what the saving rate is under CHIP?
We know that the program has been inefficient, Mr. Speaker. It has saved less energy than was anticipated by the government. We also recognize that a number of fly-by-night contractors got into the act. Workers have been poorly trained and in some cases standards of performance were low. UFFI is now installed in 125,000 homes in Canada and the government is now going to conduct a study on 2,000 of those homes. What about the other 123,000? In Ontario the provincial government has decided to study 30,000 homes.
Canadian Home Insulation Program
How many dangers to the health of Canadians are the result of inadequate testing? How many homes affected are there? I am sure the government is reluctant to assume any responsibility even though it knew in 1977, through a report made to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, that there was a possible health hazard. Another study was conducted in 1979 and now there is another "expert" study. The government has decided to study the study that studied the study in 1977! This is inexcusable, Mr. Speaker.
The government knows that the home owner's matching contribution will still not be enough to insulate a home properly. It is still far short of the dollars required, on a matching basis, to insulate properly most homes in Canada. The government budgeted $265 million for a year. The bill speaks of $195 million for nine months. I would advise the people of Canada right now that if they are going to insulate homes up to and including December 1977-not 1961 but 1977 as the bill says-there is not enough money in the bill for that.
The homes in Canada that need to be insulated will not be unless everyone starts in July and continues to insulate at maximum capacity. The installers tell me that it is physically impossible to do it. As I say, there is not enough money provided by the bill, but that is typical of the government. Perhaps when the time comes that more money is needed, it will just wind up the presses.
The loose regulations that affect the control of material that goes into the insulation of a home have resulted in only 20 per cent cut in home heating fuel consumption rather than the 30 per cent that was projected. Where is the other 10 per cent? I have not seen a report that explains why the government has fallen 33 per cent short of its objective. Canada is still the highest per capita fuel oil user in the world. If the government thinks that it is moving toward self-sufficiency by creating a National Energy Program that is causing the taps to be turned off, and if it is satisfied with paying $ 16-odd a barrel to the west and $40-odd to Mexico, Venezuela, Kuwait and Argentina, then I wish it would explain the economics of that decision. Would it not be better to spend that money in Canada to create energy and investment dollars and help us achieve self-sufficiency by 1990?
Shunning the Canadian Standards Association, the government barged ahead in 1980 by formulating its own peculiar brand of restrictions and standards for insulating contractors. I wonder how many members of the government talked to insulating contractors. The contractors will have to be college graduates if they want to pass the test set for them by the Canadian General Standards Board. A number of competent installers of insulation in my area tell me that they find it very difficult, even with the expertise they have gained through years of work, to get a pass mark on the examination set by the government. The CGSB does not have a good track record, in view of the UFFI disaster. If the government is building its hopes on an insulation program based on the record of the CGSB, it should keep in mind the disaster of UFFI which is evident in cities all across the country. The CGSB has a poor track record, Mr. Speaker.

June 30, 1981
Canadian Home Insulation Program
Canadians are off to a slow start in home renovation. The government owes it to the people to provide reliable information on its fast-spreading and obviously non-productive practices in insulating homes. Only 32 per cent of Canadian homes were built before 1950 and only 8 per cent were built before 1900. This means that 60 per cent of homes have been built since 1950. The problems that the government has with CHIP and its "ugly sister", UFFI, are really inexcusable. People who thought they were saving energy and increasing the value of their homes now find that they have potentially serious health hazards in the air of their homes and they have watched the value of their homes plummet.
I can tell the House of cases in Peterborough, Mr. Speaker, where people have sold their homes because of this government program. They had their homes well insulated with UFFI, sold their homes and established closing dates, moved out of their homes into temporary quarters or, in one case, permanent quarters, only to find that the buyers refused to close the deal because of urea formaldehyde foam insulation.
The government has been batting this around for several months-or several years-knowing full well that there would possibly be a health problem with foam insulation. Its reaction to this possible health problem was to continue studying it. The study committees are now called "expert" committees on UFFI or foam insulation. Is this telling us that in 1977 the doctor who reported to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that there was a possible health problem with foam insulation was not an expert? Is the government telling us that in 1979, when the tests were carried out on UFFI which indicated a problem, they were somewhat inadequate? I suggest that we look closely at Bill C-75 and its possible inadequacies.
In reality, the government has fallen down on four points. It takes three to four times the amount of the grant established to insulate properly a three or four-bedroom home.
It has given conflicting advice on what the best insulation is. Probably 125,000 people in Canada today thought at one time that UFFI was the best form of insulation to instal. There are innumerable stories from consumers about rip-offs by fraudulent insulation contractors.
If the government is going to enter the marketplace and suddenly become expert in giving advice to the provinces and the regions of this country on what is the best insulation to put into their homes, it should be creating the legislation and the climate in which the free enterprise system can function. The government should rely more closely on the business community to do a job that is satisfactory in the insulation business. Price will take care of itself.
Subsidization of programs by government creating a lesser cost is not always the answer to conservation. I do not think General Motors was convinced to stop building large cars with air conditioners because the government of this country decided to tax that corporation if it put in air conditioners. I think what caused people to buy smaller cars in Canada and forced
Canadian manufacturers to build smaller cars is the price of energy. If energy is priced realistically and if the charge for it is what it is worth, then the marketplace will take care of these things in a much better fashion than the bureaucrats in Ottawa.
When the government gets into such programs as CHIP the paper burden increases. A large portion of the money that is spent on the saving of energy across Canada is used by this government to feed the octopus, with its insatiable appetite for tax dollars to keep the flow of paperwork going. What happens to the business community is that every time the government passes these regulations and every time the government puts more pressure on the business community to live within the guidelines set by government, more paperwork is created. As a result, we have higher costs, higher inflation and less employment.
Nothing but confusion surrounds this government's maze of acrimonious acronyms. Only one thing comes to the public's mind when the government's energy conservation programs are announced, and that is confusion. Instead, it should be conservation. Obviously, in the absence of a coherent program for fair and stabilized Canadian oil prices, energy conservation should be the number one priority in this country.
Canadians must be helped, not hindered. Government should create the atmosphere and the climate in which the business community can function. The government should not become part of the business community. I thought the government would have learned that in 1978 with the Enersave program. At that time the government thought it could hire unemployed people to supervise and instal insulation in homes Canada, only to find out that it cost twice as much as if the government had allowed the free enterprise system to do it living within the framework of a truly competitive market.
First of all, the CHIP grant should not be a taxable benefit. Second, a $500 grant is hardly a realistic sum today to insulate properly a home in Canada. Third, there are obviously positive benefits to the business, both at the contractor level and at the wholesaler level-I know it bothers some of the socialists to hear this-and as a result of spin-offs, of an increased rate of insulation under CHIP.
CMHC, one of the major Crown corporations of this government which used to run this program, reported that at meetings held in 1977 with representatives of the major insulation manufacturing companies, federal officials were informed that a substantial increase in production could take place for all types of insulation products. Isn't that nice?
Fourth, there is such an evident lack of cohesion in the government's conservation policies that the people of this country could be forgiven for insulating their ears against the government's continued platitudes-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Pursuant to an order made earlier today, I must interrupt the hon. member because his time has expired. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) has the floor.
June 30, 1981

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to represent the New Democratic Party in speaking to Bill C-75. I must say first that I certainly agree with the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) about many of the things he said, except his last reference to socialists, of course. But I do question the very oversimplistic and astounding statements that were made in the introductory remarks on behalf of the government. This is an act dealing with CHIP for certain provinces in Canada and asks for, I believe, another estimated $65 million for this part of the program. Later we will have a bill for other provinces.
Let us take a look at CHIP, which is the federal government's effort to encourage conservation in Canadian homes. We agree it would be desirable to have a conservation program. We agree with the theoretical goals as they are stated. But the practical experience with CHIP surely falls far, far short of what the intent was.
I will deal with the information part of the program. If we look at the cost of administering this program through CMHC, a considerable amount is required just to put out basic information. The basic information is not practical. It does not get to most Canadians. It is up to Canadians to try and locate these fancy pamphlets. The information does not really advise people in a sound way on the best and safest ways to insulate homes. Seminars are not provided, for example, which would be a sound way for CMHC to give this information. In fact, misinformation has been given. Letters were sent out to consumers begging them to insulate their homes. Many of them insulated with UFLI. People were then sent letters of congratulation by CMHC and government officials for using UFFI. But all the time they were poisoning their environment.
I will deal now with the economic incentives. We have heard that up to approximately $500 is available per household. Homes built before 1977 will now be eligible. The parliamentary secretary did not elaborate on this point at all. We hear that 10 per cent of home owners have received CHIP grants. I am very glad that I am not one of the householders which has a CHIP form of insulation in my home because I think in many cases anxiety has been created by having used it. The goal is to actually upgrade some 70 per cent of Canadian homes by 1987.
I agree with my colleague who spoke earlier that Canadians must have a much sounder guarantee that they will have decent service from people who instal insulation in their homes and that certification will come from the government that the insulation is sound and reliable.
We have heard also about the many fly by night contractors. Hardly a day goes by in my area of Vancouver without phone calls from contractors who ask: "Have you got your free insulation yet? We will put it in for you for $50". We know they are taking advantage of this program. There is no real guarantee that they are reliable. In many cases they have proven to be anything but reliable. The grant itself of $500 would barely cover the cost of insulating a ceiling. Most of the home owners to whom I have spoken are most concerned
Canadian Home Insulation Program
because they have urea formaldehyde insulation. Because they cared very much for their homes they worked very hard to insulate them carefully. They spent about $2,000 for insulation in the walls of their homes. Most of that sum was their own money, but they found out they were paying for extreme problems.
We can conclude that because $500 does not nearly cover the cost of adequate insulation in a home, most pensioners and lower income people have not used this program. For once they are on the right side of things. For once the poor people have an advantage. At least they have not been poisoned by having urea formaldehyde in their homes.
This brings me to the whole question on which I want to spend most of my time. I want to have in the record the whole history relating to government responsibility for the UFFI type of insulation.
I was astounded that the parliamentary secretary when talking about the marvellous values of CHIP did not mention the health hazards of this foam. There is considerable documentation on it, and I will get to that in a minute. There is not only the threat to humans but the economic problem.
In my constituency there are many people who have worked all their lives to be able to buy a home. The savings they have been able to accumulate have gone into insulation. Now they cannot live in those homes because of the effects of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. They are faced with economic problems, health hazards, stress and anxiety. Many thousands of people across this country are angry because they have been victimized as a result of this insulation program.
Responsibility for the UFFI problem falls directly on the shoulders of the federal government which approved UFFI despite the warnings. It pushed this type of insulation through its CHIP program and praised those who used it. The health hazard was acknowledged in the ban instigated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in 1981.
I am sorry the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is not here this evening. He has acknowledged the serious problems. I wish to quote some of what he said on June 1. He stated that the federal government may offer home owners financial aid to replace the potentially hazardous insulation urea formaldehyde as a result of a random telephone survey of 800 homes. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) certainly has not supported this position. He was quoted as saying, "I would never have it in my home". Perhaps the minister showed some good judgment in that instance.
The energy minister stated that if the survey indicated there was concrete evidence the insulation was causing harmful side effects to residents, the government may consider financial aid to replace the insulation. He said that the government would take what steps are necessary. It is time those steps were considered and the budget was allocated for removing this poisonous type of foam insulation. That is the only solution for many of these home owners.

June 30, 1981
Canadian Home Insulation Program
I wish to place on record a chronological review of the problems and the different steps the government has taken in relation to UFFI. This material was first used in Canada in 1969. It was removed a year later because of shrinkage and instability problems. In 1976 the National Research Council issued warnings to the effect that the standards for UFFI were not adequate. In 1977 doctors warned of health problems. It was also in 1977 that the Canadian government approved the use of UFFI. Consumer demand was immediate as the insulation was accepted for use under the government's Canadian home insulation program. In fact, the government was pushing UFFI.
American studies and reports in the 1970s identified instances of medical problems and structural deterioration of buildings after installation of UFFI. A temporary ban was announced by the Department of National Flealth and Welfare last December and a permanent ban on April 23. I wish I had time to quote from the report of the special committee established by health and welfare.
There are many items in the April, 1981, final report of the Department of National Health and Welfare expert advisory committee on urea formaldehyde foam insulation. There are many points in the report which substantiate the danger to both health and the environment. It is very interesting since the government talks a lot about testing. That is the way of getting itself off the hook. I quote from page 8 of the report:
The committee has reservations over the usefulness of single ambient formaldehyde measurements. There can be both variations in the day, as well as from day to day variations. Changes in temperature and humidity can affect the readings. Therefore, the significance of a single reading can be misleading-
The committee is therefore not prepared to recommend any level of formaldehyde exposure as inherently safe.
That statement by an expert committee of the government emphasizes that testing one week may show a result quite different from testing the next week, not to mention six months later. Therefore, it does not solve the problem. The health hazard increases as the foam gets older. As it disintegrates, there is more likelihood of the gas affecting the residents of the home.
It is estimated that between 80,000 and 100,000 homes have UFFI. Experts agree that health problems depend on the duration of exposure and the concentration of formaldehyde. It varies as the foam gets older and according to the condition of those living in the house.
Resembling hardened shaving cream, UFFI can break down soon after installation, releasing formaldehyde gas. Symptoms include eye, nose and throat irritation, nosebleeds, headaches, coughing, nausea, asthma-like reactions, vomiting and dizziness. UFFI has been related to cancer in laboratory animals.
Elderly home owners who have visited my office have told me about having to sleep in their cars for several weeks because of the condition of their homes. They have beautiful homes but cannot live in them because of the gas concentrations caused by UFFI. Another example is two elderly people having to live in their basement. The woman has severe health problems. These people are desperate. They do not know what
to do. They cannot get any satisfaction from the government. Their anxieties and health problems are complicating the situation.
The federal government continues to stress that only a few homes will require complete removal of the foam. We do not know that. In most cases they say a few less complicated measures will reduce the exposure to the formaldehyde to near normal levels. There is no proof of that. In fact, the report from which I just quoted indicates the reverse.
Residents in my constituency and throughout the Vancouver area as well as in other cities across Canada are organizing. They are angry. These people are well informed about this issue. They have done their homework. They have the research.
Federal officials have continually said that people are unnecessarily alarmed about this. If we lived in a home with UFFI we would be alarmed as well. We would insist on more than just information which, incidentally, is not yet available.
1 have already mentioned that in adverse conditions, where many factors come into play, UFFI can cause very serious problems; high temperatures and high humidity which are of great concern in my area, along with poor ventilation and sloppy installation, usually result in the foam having to be removed. We know how inefficient many of the installers have been under the CHIP program. I think it is pretty safe to assume that the installation was faulty in many cases.
The federal government initially telephoned some 800 homes but we have not heard the results of that phone survey. Many of us have asked questions in the House as to why the government was doing this, but presumably it was to determine the extent of the problem.
Federal officials have repeatedly dismissed any legal responsibility but have admitted some moral responsibility. I am not a lawyer but I cannot see why there would not be a legal responsibility since the government itself endorsed and promoted this poisonous type of insulation.
Finally, we find that on June 11 the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs announced he was going to spend $5 million to establish an information line, a co-ordinating centre with a phone that was put into service today, I believe. There was to be a national testing of 4,000 homes. That testing is not really going to prove anything valid. There is to be a board of review set up on June 29 primarily to hear complaints from the industry which is trying to defend its position, just as is the government.
Home owners and, I am sure, landlords who have this problem in their buildings are up in arms. I have received countless letters about this and I have many clippings that I do not have time to read into the record, all of which indicate how really appalled and angry are home owners across the country. What they need is that $5 million and money from the CHIP program put into sound programs to remove this poisonous
June 30, 1981

foam from the walls of their homes, getting rid of this risk forever.
For that reason I have spent this time talking about UFFI in relation to the CHIP program. I cannot really understand in conscience how we can endorse more money in these estimates for expenditure on a foam insulation program which has not worked and for which the government has assumed no responsibility, a program that has not provided any protection to the consumer and which has been a major health problem for consumers.
We have raised these questions in the House, as have members of the Conservative party. We have made a number of recommendations. First and foremost is the importance of allocating funds for the removal of this foam from these poisoned homes. We agree it is long overdue that installers must be certified. Sometimes I think many of the CMHC and government officials should be certified as well. How the parliamentary secretary could be so innocuous in his remarks tonight by assuming this has been a sound program is beyond me.
We also question the cost of administering this program, and I will come back to this point later in relation to the CHIP program in the maritimes. A very high percentage of the allocation of funds has gone to the cost of administration by CMHC, yet when people phone CMHC about problems with contractors or UFFI they get no help at all.
A few weeks ago I directed a question to the minister responsible for CMHC and appealed to him to have CMHC through its local offices attempt to be helpful to these consumers. Surely that is reasonable since CMHC sponsored the CHIP program initially, as a result of which this foam was put into houses. It seems to me not too much to expect that people with serious health problems who cannot live in their homes until something is done about the situation, like the couple I mentioned, or those who cannot afford to live anywhere else and cannot put their homes on the market because there is no value, should be provided with some kind of alternate accommodation on an emergency basis through CMHC.
As I said earlier, we feel the government must concentrate not so much on testing but on getting this foam out of homes. There is enough proof that it is dangerous and that the hazard worsens as time goes on. Anyone with foam in their homes should be worried about it. Any real estate person would certainly be reluctant to sell a house which was, in effect, poisoned by this foam. We feel there should be tax deductions for people who take the initiative of removing the foam themselves. There should be tax credits in the case of lower income people who take this action.
Most of all I urge the minister, who is not here tonight but who said he would take note of our representations, to consider that his department should do. He is promoting this program through the bill we are discussing tonight. The federal government has continued to push home insulation programs. There are no guarantees at all that any other programs in the future will provide protection for consumers or that they will be sound insulation programs. There is no accurate information
Canadian Home Insulation Program
being given out to people and, in short, consumers are really quite disillusioned with the whole service of the federal government.
Perhaps there will be five minutes for the parliamentary secretary to respond. I urge the government through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to make some financial commitment for the removal of the foam already installed through the CHIP program, and I urge the government not to proceed with further insulation until that is done or funds to be used for that are made available as a first priority.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in an attempt to facilitate our work this evening I was brief in my introductory comments. Clearly I set a standard which could not be achieved by others in that there was a certain amount of indulgence in statements which hardly accord with the facts of the CHIP program. I note that the hon. member for Peterborough, (Mr. Domm) who indulged himself in such a cacophony of contradiction and calumny and confusion, and who has in fact left the House, evidently did not wish to hear the facts of the case with regard to the CHIP program. He made his little statements, his allegations, his half-truths and confused remarks, and then left the House. Be that as it may, I shall respond to a few of his comments in the hope that he might actually take the trouble on some occasion to seek out the facts rather than to indulge himself in the way he did.
I regret in particular that the hon. member evidently feels conservation is not a laudatory goal for a government to pursue, and if it happens at all it somehow should be left to the private sector. That point of view seems to me to avoid entirely the question of what the consumer in Canada is to do when faced with higher oil prices. People, especially in lower income groups require, need and benefit from the off-oil program which the minister described this afternoon, and from the CHIP program we have been discussing this evening. Quite obviously, conservation is the quickest, most enduring, most effective and cheapest way of reducing the consumption of energy in Canada, and to hear the hon. member attack that program strikes me as a form of reprehensible irresponsibility.
I suggest that when the member opposite, the hon. member for Peterborough, speaks about the lack of any evidence of the benefits of the program, he overlooks entirely the situation in Canada today. In fact, during the first quarter of 1981 the consumption of oil in eastern Canada dropped by 7 per cent, an extraordinary reduction in a very short time. Here is ample evidence not only of the benefits of the industrial conservation program, on which I touched earlier this evening, but also of the success of CHIP, which has substantially reduced the consumption of home heating oil across Canada, and particularly in eastern Canada.
Not only does the hon. member opposite overlook the reductions in demand which I have mentioned, but he also has paid no heed at all to the savings which have resulted from this program. I noted earlier that over $2 billion in imported oil

June 30, 1981
Canadian Home Insulation Program
costs have been saved as a result of CHIP. These are substantial savings, which will only increase in the future as the program expands. Those are macro numbers and, impressive though they are, they overlook the benefit to the average householder. Good insulation can cut heating costs by at least 30 per cent. Effective insulation can reduce projected home heating costs in 1981 by $230 for oil, $250 for electricity and $180 for natural gas. Quite obviously those savings are of substantial benefit to the consumer across our country, and especially to those, as I mentioned earlier, in the lower income categories. We are providing the opportunity for them to receive benefits and to receive incentive from the government, and we are doing it in a very effective way.
That is not to say, as seems to be the case in the minds of some members of the opposition, that CHIP is intended to meet the full costs of insulation. Not at all; it was never intended to do so, and it does not do so. What the program does is to provide assistance, incentive and impetus for householders across Canada to undertake further insulation and to provide the base cost to assist in such initiative.
Some mention was made about the fact that at the moment under the program only houses built prior to 1961 are eligible. That is true, but it has equally been noted and should be stressed that it is the intention of the government to move that date forward to 1977 at a time when we are satisfied that houses built prior to 1961 are insulated to a more substantial degree than they are at the moment.
With regard to the review of CHIP, a number of aspects of the program are under review. The study which has been referred to is to evaluate the impact of the program on the householder and on the insulation industry and to study how the delivery system might be streamlined. There will be a review of eligible items under CHIP, for example, the impact on rented units and generally the effectiveness of the program as it now stands in meeting its objectives.
I will be very brief in discussing abuse of the program. I refer the hon. member for Peterborough to a statement I made in the House some month or six weeks ago, at which time I reviewed the efforts which have been made to ensure that there is no abuse and, where such abuse has been identified, to bring those abusing the system to the courts.
A number of the comments made tonight should be dealt with. I hope there will be another occasion when we can go into this subject in some greater detail. However, I am conscious that time is passing and that we need to proceed also with our examination of the third bill before us this evening.
With regard to UFFI, upon which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) spent a great deal of time and made some rather broad statements, I only emphasize to the hon. member that the government has acted to establish a UFFI centre which is now operational. Members of the public can register their complaints or solicit information there. I think the hon. member said there was no toll-free line available. In fact there is.
What does it do? How does it help?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Those who have taken the trouble to look at the advertisements in the newspapers will see that that service is now available. A national testing survey is under way. It will ensure that the facts of the case are better understood. A board of review has been put in place to hear submissions from the industry.
Finally, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has stated quite clearly that the government will decide on any further action once the results of the national testing survey, the recommendations of the board of review and the findings of the co-ordination centre are available.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief but I promise the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) to preserve the pith and substance all the same.
The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) was asking earlier for some substantiation as to whether the programs were working and I am very happy to offer him some facts and figures from the Atlantic provinces. It is important to note that, as of June 1, 1981, over 70 per cent of eligible units in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia have participated in the program, with the resulting expenditure of almost $7 million.
A recent evaluation of the home insulation program in Nova Scotia indicated 60 per cent of participants experienced an average 9 per cent decrease in fuel consumption. This decrease varied significantly with the kind of work done. Insulating walls, for example, results in a 20 per cent decrease, whereas those installing storm doors or windows resulted in about a 20 per cent decrease. The government of Prince Edward Island has calculated that the use of heating oil there has declined by 25 per cent since 1976, primarily due to the use of the home insulation program as well as an increase in the use of wood energy and the installation of temperature setback devices.
The home insulation program was initially to end as of December 31, 1981. In view of the high participation rate it
Maritime Home Insulation Program
will proceed as planned. We are, however, examining the feasibility of extending CHIP after December 31 to those residents of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia who would be eligible and who have not participated in the home insulation program.
In 1977 it was stated the home insulation program could save a maximum of 2,500,000 barrels of oil annually. At the current international price of $44 a barrel, this amounts to a saving of $110 million.
The total cost of the home insulation program during 1981 and 1982 is estimated at $4,300,000, of which $1,075,000 is requested in the supplementary estimate. These facts and figures prove the program is indeed working. I trust all hon. members will recognize both the past success and the future necessity of this program and appropriate the required funds. On this side of the House we are fully committed to achieving energy security for Canadians. The home insulation program is one part of a much larger picture which is Canada's energy future.
In Atlantic Canada significant progress is under way on a wide variety of fronts. In fact, I would like to read from the most recent list of approved programs in Atlantic Canada, the kind of thing being done by the federal government. In Dartmouth, space heating with a wood waste Parrsboro-made furnace is a new program just approved. The Metro Transit Commission in Dartmouth has a grant to heat with solar heat in the new transit facility. Dafron Industries Ltd. in Lunenburg is now launching a sawdust waste-burning furnace for space heating. Riverport Electric in Kingsburg-Lunenburg has received a grant to monitor the wind profile at Hirtle's Beach.
We are creating a heat sink source for the new dental school at Dalhousie university in Halifax. Interprovincial Engineering in Halifax is studying the feasibility of hydro power from municipal watersheds. And in Mabou there is a new project to evaluate a small hydro site. In all, there have been some 36 projects launched just recently in the Atlantic provinces by the federal government to make the Atlantic provinces energy secure.
I urge the House to support this bill.

The house I live in Ottawa has not been changed. It is relatively new and if I were offered CHIP I would not know what to insulate. However, we have reduced our energy consumption by about 10 per cent over the last three years because energy is darned expensive and I turned the thermostat down.
Now, I suppose my savings are going to show up in some bureaucrat's statistics so they can say "Look, CHIP is working marvellously, HIP is working marvellously, we have saved 10

per cent." Nonsense! They have not saved a darned thing as a result of the program. The saving is a result of the decision I made and similar decisions are being made by millions of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I have several questions relating to housing in the maritimes and their home insulation programs. I do not believe the minister clarified why the programs are different in the maritimes. I understand they are largely administered through the provincial governments and subsidized by the federal government. Perhaps I am wrong, but I would be interested in hearing the minister's remarks.
Also I believe that the dates which are being applied to the programs are different in the maritimes. They will receive funding to insulate homes built up to 1981, if I am not mistaken. Why is this aspect different from other parts of Canada?
Also I would be interested in knowing what other conservation methods are being promoted. What other sources of alternate energy are being promoted, such as solar heat and so on?
I believe an article appeared in The Globe and Mail today which indicated that CMHC is adopting rules on oil-heated homes which will take effect tomorrow. Particularly it was indicated that homes heated by oil will remain eligible for mortgage insurance in the four Atlantic provinces and in the two territories where the alternatives of natural gas and electricity are not available at reasonable cost. In the other provinces new oil-heated homes will not be eligible for mortgage insurance through CMHC. This seems quite reasonable. It is a good incentive, with the exceptions where they should be, in the Atlantic region.
Having visited the Atlantic provinces on a housing tour, I noted some of the housing characteristics of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and the other Atlantic provinces. There is a very high degree of home ownership. Many people do not have mortgages. Many of the homes were self-built.
Why is nothing being done to change the application of CHIP so that people can put their own labour into it? Why must they always go through contractors in whom they really do not have much confidence? Why cannot this program be adapted so that people can do it themselves? Perhaps there could be seminars or some assistance for these people to do it themselves. Then they could make sure the money is spent the way it should be. It would make sense, particularly in the maritimes where there is a tradition of building co-operatives and putting their own labour into their homes.
Also I noted that things are changing rapidly in the maritimes. This gets back to housing costs. I saw white-painting in city centres which put up the cost of housing. I think the conversion of older homes and the rehabilitation of them would certainly increase demand for home insulation. Also I noted zero vacancy rates in the larger cities. Saint John is very similar to Vancouver. I gather Halifax now has the highest percentage increase in house prices. Surely this will have an impact on the program as well.
I received a number of letters from people complaining that there was not a fair allocation of money for co-op housing in the maritimes, particularly in Nova Scotia. I would be interested to know whether there are any facts concerning the number of maritimers in these two provinces who have used UFFI. I understand there were considerable complaints in the past about problems with another type of insulation known as a cellulose fibre material. It was installed in 40 per cent of the maritime homes which used CHIP grants. This insulation can rot in Atlantic weather and affect the structural stability of houses. Pressure from insulation installers to lower test standards to allow more insulation material on the market has produced a situation similar to the UFFI problem. The problem is the same, so I will not repeat my questions.
I must say that I did not receive any serious answers from the previous government speakers. I would be interested in knowing what guarantees there will be for consumers in the extension of this program to make it available for modern houses. What compensation will there be for those people who are victims of poor insulation programs, particularly UFFI? Has the government received complaints about this from the Atlantic region?
In closing, I should like to register my concern in regard to some of the figures and estimates for these programs. Going back to the budget for this fiscal year, I note that $3,200,000 was allocated for contribution payments to individuals for the home insulation program in the two Atlantic provinces. Also I noted that the contribution payments to CMHC for administrative costs were $1,100,000. This is 35 per cent of the total
June 30, 1981

allocation for those two provinces. I think there should be some explanation why that amount of federal money is going to CMHC administration, not to the people who need home insulation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as to the first question, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia were originally selected for the insulation and energy conservation program because they required a means of offsetting the substantial increase in the cost of electrical generation resulting from their high reliance upon imported oil-fired thermal generation. This was the real reason and the urgency for the program in that area.
It was determined that the resulting expenditure burden on consumers would be greatly reduced by a policy aimed at greater efficiency in consumer use of petroleum energy in general and specifically by a program which would result in greater efficiency in space heating.
The home insulation program was first introduced in PEI. Based on the experience in that province, CMHC anticipated a good response from householders in Nova Scotia, so a decision was made to go ahead with the expanded program.
As to the second question concerning eligibility, the home insulation program applies to units built and occupied prior to January 1, 1977 in Nova Scotia and in Prince Edward Island. The eligible units include principal residences, either rented or owned; houses or apartment buildings three storeys or less; mobile homes and hostels are also eligible. A grant is provided for either the cost of materials in the amount of $350 or one-third of the total costs of labour and insulation materials to a maximum of $500. The home owner can instal it himself; there is an either/or provision. I hope I have made that clear.
A further indication of federal assistance to these particular areas of Canada, PEI and Nova Scotia, is the fact that this grant is non-taxable. There are other items included in the program, such as insulation materials, weather stripping, caulking, and the installation of storm windows and doors. Applicants go through a pre-application process to obtain approval for the proposed work prior to having the work undertaken.
I hope these are the answers the hon. member requested. At to co-operative housing, I would ask the hon. member to direct those questions to the minister responsible for CMHC.

Mr. Speaker, the circumstances under which I rise are quite unusual, I do take great pleasure and some honour in making these few remarks about Bill C-70.
What I wish to do is put before the House, as a proper preliminary to these amendments which we are now discussing, something of the history of this very important legislation which has been on the books for over 60 years. This bill is called "an Act to amend the Animal Disease and Protection Act."
As the House knows, the movement of any form of livestock or any form of plant material across borders is one of the most sensitive things in the world today. The one act that protects the producers and consumers of animals is this act which we have before us.
My first memory of this act goes back 30 years to the unfortunate outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan in 1951. At that time we had an act in place which allowed for a very small compensation for animals which were destroyed. The circumstance at that time involved a person who had been travelling in Europe, who came to work on a farm near McLean, Saskatchewan and who had apparently carried on his clothing some of the virus of this disease which we are now discussing under one of the sections of this bill. This virus caused the spread of foot-and-mouth disease, which
11118

June 30, 1981
Animal Diseases
is a very serious disease in Europe. Any mention of it in North America causes great panic in the market squares of Canada.
Foot-and-mouth disease affects all forms of animals with cloven hooves; but it also has another effect, too, and that is that it debilitates the animal. But the animal can recover. The fact remains that the spread of this virus terrifies those of us who have dealt with it.
Parliament may not know, but one of the proudest sections of the Department of Agriculture is the health of animals branch, which is made up of a group of underpaid veterinarians who have done more to build up the cattle industry in Canada than any other group, outside of the breeding section, 1 suspect. These men worked to a standstill, at great physical discomfort, to clear this country of tuberculosis.
That program went on from the early 1920s, all during the twenties, the thirties, the forties and the fifties. I had the privilege of doing the last inoculation of some 15 million animals which had been inoculated over that long period of time. Today, Canada remains free of bovine tuberculosis because of the magnificent veterinarians from all across Canada who serve in the health of animals branch. Tonight we are carrying this bill forward trying to meet with current conditions.
I introduced my remarks by talking about foot-and-mouth disease, since it strikes terror into all producers of beef, pork, etc. We have never had to endure in North America what has been endured in Europe. We are very fortunate that when this disease did break out in Canada in 1951 we had a very competent health of animals branch which moved into the battle. The battle was not that terrible because the few animals which had the infection recovered. The fact is that the virus has moved down that one creek, the Waskana Creek, through Regina and northwesterly from Regina, and got into some of the purebred herds. What made it difficult for the health of animals branch to fight the spread of that virus was the fact that the compensation in the bill at that time was so low, based on a previous period when prices of cattle were much lower, that no farmers with purebred dairy or purebred beef wanted to report any signs in their herd which would indicate the presence of that disease. They were afraid to do this because they knew the procedure was to quarantine the whole herd and, if necessary, destroy the whole herd, even if it were healthy. But because the animals had been exposed, under the rules of the game, and to win confidence in the world that we were fighting this battle, all herds were destroyed.
I do not see the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) in the House, but he would know about this because the main part of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in 1951 occurred in his area. Many of us remember these beautiful herds of dairy and beef cattle being brought in. They were some of the most beautifully bred animals I have ever seen and it was tragic to see them being lined up and shot, then dumped into pits with chemicals thrown over them. It was a cruel sight
to see, knowing that the farmer concerned had his basic herd destroyed when he knew that all the animals were healthy. It was done for a psychological reason-to prove to the Americans, who were our main market, that we would do everything possible to eliminate that disease entirely. We won the confidence of the American market and got it back in the next year or so.
Next I want to describe the very dramatic debate that took place in this House in the summer or early fall of 1951. The minister of agriculture at that time was the Right Hon. James Garfield Gardiner. He put up a sturdy battle to protect the act as it existed at that time. He had no choice but to do that. The compensation offered was too low to induce farmers to volunteer information. The member on this side of the House who led the debate was the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. For four or five days the two men fought out the issue of expanding compensation to include farmers on voluntary report, so that there would be no question of anyone losing his whole livelihood because he made this contribution to the industry. The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent settled the issue and ruled that what the then member for Lake Centre proposed should be accepted and the compensation rated to a level that the farmers would feel was equitable.
I was present during that debate and, of course, coming from the affected area, I had an intimate knowledge of all the people concerned. The experiences of that terrible summer of 1951, when foot-and-mouth disease almost threatened to destroy the beef industry of western Canada, have never left my mind.
Tonight our purpose is to amend the act, and the key issue is compensation. The provisions of the bill make all the animals listed available for compensation at market price. Two groups of diseases are exempt; one is tuberculosis, which, to my knowledge, was wiped out 20 years ago in Canada; the other is brucellosis. The reason for this is that both those diseases have direct effects on humans; in other words, the disease is trans-mittable from animals to humans. I suspect that is the reason that the health of animals branch always paid special attention to them.
It is regrettable that even though the level of compensation is increased in the bill to the market price for all animals, a different technique is used for animals suffering from tuberculosis and brucellosis. It is commendable to raise the amount over what it has been for the last five or six years, but it still does not meet the experience of the last 50 years.
In the last four or five years brucellosis came from Manitoba into my riding so I have some experience in this area. I have seen herds of 700 cattle slaughtered when I doubt if any more than two or three of the cattle had ever been infected. I saw a family forced to feed their animals in a closed area under quarantine. They could not put them out to pasture where there would be contact across the fence with other animals or other grass, because the virus spreads by contact with grass, grain, mud and so on. After the winter feed was gone, the farmer had to haul grain and water. Eventually he had to borrow thousands of dollars every week in order to bring in
June 30, 1981

feed and water for his animals. He was not allowed to sell them. The family almost went into bankruptcy.
Thanks to help from the health of animals branch, I was able to get through to the government the fact that this farmer should be helped. If the health of animals branch wanted to keep that herd under quarantine, then I thought it was its responsibility to feed and water them and to keep the farmer and his family from going broke. The branch finally accepted this argument and on the instructions of the chief in Ottawa gave the order to slaughter the whole herd even though they knew that, if they waited long enough and no more cases of infection occurred, the herd would have been cleared and left intact.
There are not many animals on that farm today and a lot of the barns have been burned down; but the farmer hopes it can be rehabilitated and again become one of the major cattle producing farms of Saskatchewan.
This bill makes the mistake that has been made every time this situation has occurred in the last 50 years. A fixed amount has been set for compensation for brucellosis and tuberculosis. A fixed amount is dangerous, Mr. Speaker. If the price of cattle is above that set by legislation when brucellosis occurs, the farmer will have a feeling of being discriminated against, as was the case with outbreaks of foot and mouth disease and when we were fighting the outbreak of brucellosis which came from Manitoba to Saskatchewan. It is not possible for legislation to establish the value of our cattle at the moment they are to be killed.
I know nothing can be done at this late date, but Treasury Board must learn that it is necessary to include a flexible formula based on the market price for an average period of quarantine so that the farmer will not be subject to the whims of the only buyer who is allowed to buy. He will not get a fair market price when there is only one buyer. The packing plant that will take the animal is appointed by the health of animals branch. The minute the animals go through the gate, they are subject to the packers' price.
Even though the amount of compensation is fixed, if, as I expect to happen in the next two or three years, cattle prices increase from the 70 cents to 80 cents per 100 pounds live weight at present to over $2, that would make a 1,000 pound animal worth $2,000 or $2,220. It would be a blow to the farmer to have to accept $1,200 each for several hundred animals that have to be slaughtered. Often they would represent a lifetime of work.
I should have liked to see the bill include a formula which stated that the market value would apply to cases of brucellosis and tuberculosis, based on the number of days the farm was in quarantine and giving the average price for that period. If that price were flexible and moved up and down with the market, it would encourage every farmer who had a suspicion of something wrong with his herd to report it. If he saw a cow abort he would report it immediately because of the possibility of brucellosis. If he does report it and finds that it is brucellosis, the whole herd is condemned as well as all the other herds who have been in contact through fences, neighbouring pas-
Animal Diseases
tures or sharing a common pasture. The loss effect, economically and otherwise, is tremendous.
I think it would be wise for us to remember the next time we amend this bill that Parliament should have a little more time to get amendments through. I know that the health of animals branch wants a flexible formula, but I also know that Treasury Board works on very fixed principles protecting the public purse. I know the reasons for the arguments on both sides. We are not doing credit to the whole purpose of this bill by putting in the section with maximums in it. Whatever the maximum is, it is generous now for the average type of animal, but it does not allow for exotics and above all it does not allow for the rise and fall of the price structure. That is the essential weakness in the bill which has been there ever since the beginning, even though we are generous in raising the amounts at various times in the life of this bill; but the fact is it should be flexible to make sure there is no sense of loss, inequality or injustice whatever. It is imperative to those who are trying to build up the cattle industry, indeed to the survival of the human race, that there be no hesitation on the part of a farmer in reporting anything unusual.
These diseases can be damaging and devastating, affecting whole continents and the lives of thousands of people. I would think in introducing this bill on behalf of the minister that the minister should be as straightforward as I have tried to be in saying that this bill has good points but also this one fatal weakness.
I know the health of animals branch has for three years had before Treasury Board the proposal respecting a flexible formula. I am sorry they did not get it. I am sometimes tempted to suggest very strong action by ministers when they run into this type of situation. We all agree, regardless of party affiliation, on what should be done, but we run into this hurdle every time because the legalistic-minded people who draft these bills do not think about what the health of animals branch has to face in dealing with these terribly contagious diseases which can do so much harm in a short space of time.
I will not horrify the House with examples of what I have seen in this field. I simply say that I am glad that we have been able to get this bill into this House, even if it has been two or three years in the making. We are glad to put it through but with the warning of what is going to happen as sure as we are all sitting here.
I hope any other person who wants to discuss this bill will bring forward the other aspects that I know are lacking in the bill. I can think of a few but others may want to speak to them.
I was supposed to speak until Black Rod knocked on the door. May I continue, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to register my total dissatisfaction with the answers I received to two very important questions earlier today during the question period. One deals with the matter of grain transportation and the matter of rolling stock, and the other with the railway capacity problem, particularly as it relates to western Canada. Both of these issues, to me, are issues in which the government is failing very dramatically.
I should like to deal first with the matter of the grain carrying fleet. What is happening is that the boxcar fleet dedicated to the movement of grain is decreasing very rapidly. In 1980 there were some 28,400 pieces of rolling stock composed of 14,400 boxcars and 14,000 hopper cars. That boxcar fleet is declining at the rate of about 1,000 cars per year with respect to the CNR and 800 cars per year with respect to the CPR. This means that at the end of this year, 1981, there will be 3,600 fewer cars in the grain carrying fleet than in 1980.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in his answer today said there is no need for more hopper cars. I should point out that in the 1979-80 crop year we were able to move some 23 tonnes with roughly 28,000 pieces of rolling stock. What is happening is that the movement of grain both for export position and for commercial position in Canada is now declining. We are now faced with an uneviable record of moving less grain in this country than we did last year at the same time. I should like to put these figures on the record.
The total commercial disappearance of Canadian grain from August 1 to June 10, 1981 is recorded at 23.674 million tonnes. For 1980 over the same period, August 1 to June 11, that figure was recorded at 23.882 million tonnes. I should point out that while we are about 100,000 tonnes ahead in export disappearance we are about 285,000 tonnes behind in commercial disappearance. So we are falling behind now and

Yet at the same time the Minister of Transport said in the House today that it is the view of the government, based on a number of studies, that there is no need for more hopper cars this year. It's an absolutely urgent priority . . . It's the most important priority we're facing.
Today in the House the Minister of Transport pooh-poohed the idea. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said we should not have laughed at double tracking. I have read the Senate debates for June 29 at page 2638 in relation to double tracking, a matter raised in the other place. This is what the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board had to say about double tracking:
Many people felt that this statement was rather foolish and farfetched.
The commitment of the Prime Minister was to double track the line from Winnipeg to Vancouver using the existing sidings. I have to agree with the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board on that.
I want to know what the government is going to do. Will it stand idly by and do nothing about the capacity problem, recognizing that there is to be a 70 per cent increase in traffic demand in western Canada? Will it do nothing about finding
Adjournment Debate
adequate revenues for the railways for the movement of grain? Will it allow our reputation as a reliable supplier of grain and other export commodities once again to deteriorate? In short, is it the policy of the government simply to stand idly by and allow this policy of rationing, which has been talked about by the railways, to take place, or is it going to do something about it? If it is, would it please tell this House what plans it has? It owes that explanation to the House.
It owes it to this House, the people of Canada and particularly the producers and those people who rely upon the movement of export commodities to port position for movement to other countries. It owes it to everyone to lay its plans before this House and the country so that we can get on with the job of building, providing jobs and strengthening the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised several issues related to the adequacy of western rail capacity to meet the anticipated demand, especially from bulk commodities, in the coming years. In a sense some of these issues are peripheral to the main issue. For example, it is obvious that the government will have to look at the need for additional grain hopper cars in the near future, but the general view in the grain industry is that an order does not have to be placed immediately.
The hon. member seemed to object to a press report in which Senator Perrault was quoted. Without knowing exactly what the Senate leader said, it is clear, even from the press report, that he was talking about possible rationing by the railways, not Ottawa, and that this could occur in 1985 if decisions are not made soon. These distinctions, however, are not very comforting for the producer of coal, potash or grain who will be faced with congestion and bottlenecks. The main issue here is that bottlenecks will occur, and rationing is unavoidable unless railways obtain sufficient revenue to invest soon in increased rail capacity.
The hon. member has correctly identified this as the critical problem. Others, including the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in his speech last fall in Edmonton, have also done so. What they have recognized is that the debate, which started as a discussion on what to do with the Crow rate, has now evolved and broadened to a global concern for western economic development. As everyone knows, the western economy depends heavily on the export of raw materials. If the transportation system does not have the capacity to move them, the economy of the west, indeed of the country, will suffer.
Some months ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in the House that he was not willing to consider changes to the Crow rate unless there was a consensus in the west that changes had to be made. In my view, Mr. Speaker, more and more westerners are now realizing that this is not just an agricultural issue but one that affects western economic development in general, and they are speaking out. As a responsible westerner, I am sure the hon. member does his best each weekend to build the consensus that the government is seeking. I hope he encourages his colleagues to do the same.
