Mr. Speaker, I will attempt to deal with many of the points the hon. member made in his presentation. I will deal basically with his original question and say that, as part of the review process under the herd maintenance assistance program, an individual review of each township outside the severe drought area was undertaken.
In the first instance, this review was undertaken by the program staff as townships were identified during the initial process. A report and recommendation were prepared for each township and forwarded to the review board when it commenced operations in January, 1981. These reviews were based on all available precipitation data for each township under consideration.
During the board's initial review of some of these township files, it became apparent that the board did not concur in many of the program's staff recommendations to reject townships on the basis of precipitation levels greater than 60 per cent of normal. To resolve these disagreements it was agreed that professional hydrologists employed by PFRA would carry out rigorous regional storm analyses on all townships outside the drought area. These analyses are based on the premise that if any point within the township received less than 60 per cent of normal precipitation, the township met the program precipitation criterion. The analyses considered only basic regional storms and ignored peak storm values and localized precipitation. Based on the regional storm analyses of April 14, 1981 the review board and program staff have concurred in the inclusion in the drought area of approximately 450 townships out of the total of 1,300 townships originally identified as outside the drought area.

INDIAN AFFAIRS-DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF MANITOBA INDIAN BANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am here tonight to draw attention to a question which I asked some time ago of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). In fact, I asked the question on March 16 of this year.
Basically, what I asked the minister at that time was for an assurance that his department and he would do everything possible to meet the needs of the Indian people in Manitoba. He responded by saying that some of the matters I raised at that time had already been dealt with in meetings with Indians in Manitoba. In response to a supplementary question he said that I was becoming repetitious. If the question is becoming repetitious it is only because it has not been answered. What is the government doing to meet the needs of Indian people In Manitoba? I will continue to raise this question until it is answered in a real way.
All it takes for any citizen, including the minister or any of his representatives, is to look at the conditions of the Indian people in Manitoba, as they are common across this country. They have only to look at the social conditions, the economic conditions and the financial status of Indian people to see that the question has not been answered.
One might ask oneself whether this is really an important question, since it is not a new question and the conditions are almost perennial. As a Canadian I say that it is very important since it remains a blot on our social landscape. It is a matter of shame that in the history of our country we have allowed the disparities which exist between the Indian people and the general population to become so broad. I say that the government is wrong in not acting to reduce these disparities. I feel the people of this country are willing to pay the price necessary to allocate financial resources to reduce those disparities, and to reduce them in a significant way.
Today, in preparation for tonight, 1 spoke to the Indian leaders in Manitoba to obtain an update on their meetings with the minister and with regard to whether or not the minister had turned around and started to take some real action. Unfortunately, what I found is that the Indian leaders
Adjournment Debate
in Manitoba still have a plethora of unmet priorities to which the minister has been unable to respond.
Even though this may sound unkind, 1 must say that while the minister has often met with the Indian people he does not seem to possess the capacity to deliver. He makes commitments, comes back and meets with his officials but does not seem to know how to deliver the goods. This is something which bothers the Indian people of Manitoba and the Indian people across this country. I know, because it is brought to my attention quite often.
When I spoke to the Indian leaders today they indicated to me a whole list of priorities which remain unmet. I only have time to mention a few. For example, there are 61 Indian reserves in Manitoba which have been promised 20 new schools between now and 1990. The other 41 reserves will have to wait for the promise of a school until after 1990.
The same situation prevails with regard to child welfare. The province has the jurisdictional responsibility but will only act in life and death situations. The federal government, through the Department of Indian Affairs, does not have any services to provide for child welfare. Indian people have been developing proposals to present so that they can deliver these services themselves, but there has not been sufficient response from the government.
It goes on, into water rights, migratory birds and economic development. For example, I know that the department recently made a proposal to give billions of dollars for economic development on Indian reserves. It was turned down. Then it went scrambling for a shopping list of projects for Manitoba that could come within the limited budget being offered by cabinet. Of course, the shopping list was developed without the involvement of the Indian leadership in Manitoba. This is another example of how needs are not being met. They cannot be met unless the people concerned are involved.
I am rushing along, Mr. Speaker, because of the shortage of time but I want to say that a big, splash announcement was made recently in Winnipeg about an increase of 33 per cent for band core funding across the country. That amounted to $3.8 million and is the only increase since 1972. When inflation is taken into account it is in a fact a decrease. This is another example of funds not meeting the needs.
The Winnipeg Indian council has as its priority the core funding for its organization. I understand that the minister has promised action on this and we are giving him until July 14 to deliver on that promise. I hope in this instance he can demonstrate the capacity to deliver the goods once he has made a commitment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the concern of the hon. member on this question. It has tremendous ramifications and covers a broad spectrum of the concerns of native peoples.

June 30, 1981
Adjournment Debate
While the government recognizes its responsibility to Indian people and its commitment to provide financial support in response to their needs, it must also recognize that this must be done within the confines of available resources.
The House should recognize the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's strong commitment to looking for new ways to deal with increased budgetary restraints and higher costs of providing this support. The department is coming up with solutions to problems identified at the band level, such as the housing subsidy which the department was responsible for increasing last year.
Although the government recognizes its responsibility for Indian residents in Canada, those Indian people living off the reserve must also be recognized as citizens of the provinces in which they are residing. Therefore, the federal government is continuing to attempt to work out solutions with the provincial governments whereby they recognize their responsibility as well for these Canadian residents. Jurisdiction for status Indians, in particular, living off the reserve is a question which will take much negotiation and time on both sides to work out.
With particular reference to the Manitoba situation and the request made by the chiefs for the resignation of our senior managers there, I wish to reiterate that we have every confidence in those members of the departmental staff of Indian
Affairs and Northern Development. Public servants must take critical decisions every day, and will continue to be subject to this kind of publicity in light of those decisions.
Consultation with the bands continues, and I am fully confident that the proper consultation processes are being implemented. Other groups are welcome to participate in these discussions and their concerns may be addressed in that forum, if they wish to make those concerns known to our regional management team for their consideration.
The hon. member mentioned that the recent 33 per cent increase in funding for Indian bands to cover the expenses of chief and counsellor was another example of the department's failure to keep its commitment. I would say that the $3,800,000 goes a lot further in keeping a commitment than was the case before the money was granted. I think the department, and the minister in particular, is making a very honest attempt to meet the concerns of the hon. member and native problems, and he will continue to do so.
